Title: How to Configure Filter & Group by in Odoo 18 Using XML?
Content:
Odoo, the powerful open-source ERP system, offers robust customization through XML views. One of the most practical and user-friendly ways to enhance the usability of list views in Odoo is to use filters and group-by options. These tools allow users to quickly find and analyze data without writing a single line of code on the front end.

 

In this blog post, we'll explore two powerful features in Odoo 18 that help users manage and analyze data effectively: Filters and Group By functionality. These tools are essential for any Odoo user who wants to work efficiently with large datasets.

What are Filters in Odoo?

Filters in Odoo allow you to display only the records that match specific criteria. They help you focus on relevant data by hiding records that don't meet your conditions.

Filters are defined using domains and can be added via XML or the Odoo interface. They make it easier to manage and analyze large amounts of data precisely.

Types of Filters:

 

  • Default Filters: Predefined filters that come with standard Odoo modules (e.g., "My Pipeline", "Open Tasks").

 

  • Custom Filters: User-defined filters created on the fly or through XML for specific business needs.

 

  • Global Filters: Filters applicable across multiple views or models, often used in dashboards.

 

  • Contextual Filters: Dynamic filters that use context variables like uid, today(), or user input.

 

The right filters can reduce searching time and help users make quicker, data-driven decisions.

Group By : 

 

Group By in Odoo allows users to organize records into meaningful groups based on the values of a specific field. This functionality is especially useful for analyzing data patterns, comparing performance, and summarizing key metrics.

Creating Custom Filters in Odoo 18

Let’s say you want to improve how your team works with the Sales Orders list view in Odoo 18. To do that, you can customize the search options to make important data easier to access.

First, you want to add a filter that shows only the Sales Orders that have been invoiced. This helps users quickly find completed orders without scrolling through drafts or quotations.

Next, you want to add a Group By option so that Sales Orders can be categorized by Salesperson. This is useful for tracking individual performance or organizing orders by responsible users.

Finally, you want to make sure both of these options are visible in the search bar, so users can apply them instantly—no need to recreate filters manually or dig through menus.

This kind of customization makes the list view cleaner, faster to use, and tailored to your team’s daily workflow.

Step 1: Inherit the search View

 

Let’s start by inheriting the default search view for sale.order.

				
					sale.order.
views/sale_order_views.xml:
<odoo>
	<record id="view_sale_order_filter_inherit" model="ir.ui.view">
    	<field name="name">sale.order.filter.inherit</field>
    	<field name="model">sale.order</field>
    	<field name="inherit_id" ref="sale.sale_order_view_search_inherit_sale”/>
    	<field name="arch" type="xml">
        	<!-- Add a new custom filter -->
        	<xpath expr="//search" position="inside">
       	<filter name="invoiced_orders" string="Fully Invoiced"
      	domain="[('invoice_status','=','invoiced')]" help="Show orders that are fully invoiced."/>
            	<!--  Add a custom group by -->
            	<group expand="1" string="Group By">
                	<filter name="group_by_user" string="Salesperson" context="{'group_by': 'user_id'}"/>
            	</group>
        	</xpath>
    	</field>
	</record>
</odoo>

Now your Sales Order search bar has:

  • A new filter: “Fully Invoiced”
  • A new group option: “Salesperson”

Step 2: Set Default Filter and Group By

 

Let’s take it a step further — not only do we want to add the filter and group by options, but we also want Odoo to apply them automatically when the user opens the Sales Orders list view. In other words, the system should load the view with the “Invoiced Orders” filter and grouped by Salesperson right from the start.

There are two ways to achieve this:

Option A – Override the Existing Action

 

If you’re okay changing the default behavior:

				
					<record id="sale.action_orders" model="ir.actions.act_window">
	<field name="context">
    	{
        	'search_default_invoiced_orders': 1,
        	'group_by': 'user_id'
    	}
	</field>
</record>

Option B – Create a New Menu + Action

 

If you want a dedicated menu with the filter/grouping applied:

				
					<record id="action_orders_fully_invoiced" model="ir.actions.act_window">
	<field name="name">Invoiced Sales Orders</field>
	<field name="res_model">sale.order</field>
	<field name="view_mode">list,form</field>
	<field name="context">
    	{
        	'search_default_invoiced_orders': 1,
        	'group_by': 'user_id'
    	}
	</field>
</record>
<menuitem id="menu_fully_invoiced_orders"
      	name="Invoiced Orders"
      	parent="sale.sale_menu_root"
      	action="action_orders_fully_invoiced"
      	sequence="20"/>

Result : 

 

When the user clicks Invoiced Orders:

  • The list opens grouped by Salesperson
  • Only fully invoiced orders are shown
  • Users can still remove the filter or group by something else

Final Thoughts on Customizing Filters and Groupings in Odoo

Customizing filters and groupings in Odoo using XML is simple, user-friendly, and safe when done within your own module. It’s a powerful technique that works across all models—whether you're working in CRM, Accounting, Inventory, Projects, or even custom-built apps.

Title: How to Setup Odoo 16 Development Environment Using Pycharm in Ubuntu 22.04
Content:
Long-Term Support (LTS) version of Ubuntu 22.04, offering ongoing application updates and critical security patches for five years from its release date. Additionally, standard software updates deliver new Linux kernel versions and graphics driver updates every six months.

In this blog, we’ll set up a development environment for Odoo 16 using the PyCharm IDE on Ubuntu 22.04.

Before configuring PyCharm, we must install the essential libraries and packages required to run Odoo. Let’s go through the setup step by step.

Step 1: Install PyCharm IDE

PyCharm has three main versions: Education, Community, and Professional (previously known as Enterprise). In this tutorial, we'll set up the Community Edition, a completely free and open-source option.

 

Before you begin installation, please verify that your system meets the basic requirements to ensure PyCharm runs without issues. You can install PyCharm by downloading the Debian installation package directly from the official website or using the command line.

To install PyCharm via the command line, follow these steps:

 

Open the terminal using Ctrl + Alt + T.
Run the following commands:

				
					-> sudo apt-get update 
-> sudo apt-get upgrade
-> sudo snap install pycharm-community --classic
Step 2: Install Python 3 and Required Packages

 

To begin developing with Odoo, Python 3 must be installed along with several supporting packages. You can install Python 3 using the following command:

				
					-> sudo apt install python3-pip

You can install the necessary packages and dependencies for Python 3 using the following command:

				
					-> sudo apt-get install python3-dev build-essential libjpeg-dev libpq-dev libjpeg8-dev libxml2-dev libssl-dev libffi-dev libmysqlclient-dev libxslt1-dev zlib1g-dev libsasl2-dev libldap2-dev liblcms2-dev
Step 3: Install Web Dependencies

 

Odoo requires several web-related dependencies to support its frontend features and web client interface. You can install these dependencies using the following command:

				
					-> sudo apt-get install -y npm
-> sudo ln -s /usr/bin/nodejs/usr/bin/node 
-> sudo npm install -g less less-plugin-clean-css 
-> sudo apt-get install -y node-less
Step 4: Install wkhtmltopdf

 

Installing wkhtmltopdf is essential for generating PDF reports in Odoo, such as invoices, quotations, and other printable documents. Use the following commands to install it:

				
					-> sudo        wgethttps://github.com/wkhtmltopdf/wkhtmltopdf/releases/download/0.12.5/wkhtmltox_0.12.5-1.bionic_amd64.deb 
-> sudo dpkg -i wkhtmltox_0.12.5-1.bionic_amd64.deb 
-> sudo apt install -f
Step 5: Install PostgreSQL

 

Odoo uses PostgreSQL as its database management system. To install PostgreSQL, run the following command in the terminal:

				
					-> sudo apt-get install postgresql

Once installed, PostgreSQL will automatically start as a background service. You may also need to create a PostgreSQL user for Odoo, which we will cover in a later step.

Step 6: Create a Database User Role for Odoo

 

After installing PostgreSQL, you need to create a dedicated user role that Odoo will use to manage its databases. This user must have sufficient privileges, and you’ll also need to set a password that will later be referenced in the Odoo configuration file.

				
					-> sudo su - postgres
    createuser --createdb --username postgres --no-createrole --no-superuser --pwprompt   odoo16

Grant Superuser Privileges to the Odoo Database User

 

To ensure Odoo has full access to manage its databases and extensions, it's recommended (especially for development environments) to grant superuser privileges to the user you created.

				
					-> Psql
    ALTER USER odoo16 WITH SUPERUSER;

Exit from PostgreSQL and Switch Back to the Main User

 

Once you’ve granted superuser privileges to the Odoo user:

  1. Exit the PostgreSQL interactive terminal by typing:
				
						q 
	Exit
Step 7: Download Odoo 16 Source Code

You can obtain the Odoo 16 Community Edition source code either by downloading it directly from Odoo’s official GitHub repository or by cloning the repository using Git.

To clone the repository, first ensure that Git is installed on your system. Then, execute the following commands.

  1. Install Git (if not already installed):
				
					-> sudo apt-get install git
  1. The following command will clone the Odoo 16 source code into a directory named   odoo16       located inside your home directory:
				
					-> git clone https://www.github.com/odoo/odoo --depth 1 --branch 16.0 --single-branch  odoo16
Step 8: Install Required Python Packages

 

Odoo depends on several Python libraries, all of which are listed in the requirements.txt file located within the odoo16 directory.

To install these dependencies, follow the steps below:

  1. Navigate to the Odoo 16 source directory:
				
					-> cd odoo16
  1. Install the required Python packages using pip:
				
						-> sudo pip3 install -r requirements.txt
			OR
 -> sudo pip3 install -r /requirements.txt

Important: Ensure that all dependencies are installed correctly. Incomplete or improper installation may lead to errors during the execution and usage of Odoo in your development environment.

Step 9: Open the Odoo Project in PyCharm


Launch PyCharm Community Edition and follow these steps to open your Odoo project:

  1. From the welcome screen, click on “Open”.
  2. Navigate to your home directory and select the odoo16 folder.
  3. Click “OK” to load the project into PyCharm.

After the project loads in PyCharm, you may see a dialog box prompting you to configure a Python interpreter or set up a virtual environment, similar to the one shown in the screenshot below.

Python3.10 interpreter is supported by Ubuntu 22.04 by default, but Python 3.8 is also available.

Step 10: Create odoo.conf File Inside the odoo16 Directory

 

To configure Odoo, you’ll need to create a configuration file named odoo.conf within the root of your odoo16 directory. Follow these steps in PyCharm:

  1. Right-click on the odoo16 directory.

  2. Select New → File.

  3. Name the file odoo.conf and click OK.

Paste the following configuration block into the newly created file:

				
					[options]
; This is the password that allows database operations:
admin_passwd = admin
db_host = localhost
db_port = 5432
db_user = odoo16
db_password = your_password_here
addons_path = addons
xmlrpc_port = 8069

Note: Replace your_password_here with the actual password you set for the odoo16 PostgreSQL user during the earlier step.

If you have custom modules in a separate directory, you can include that path as well—just separate multiple paths with commas.

Example,
addons_path = /home/youruser/odoo16/odoo/addons, /home/youruser/odoo16/custom_addons

Step 11: Add Python Interpreter

 

To run Odoo from within PyCharm, you need to configure a Python interpreter for the project. Follow the steps below:

  1. Navigate to File → Settings (or Ctrl + Alt + S).

  2. In the left sidebar, go to Project: odoo16 → Python Interpreter.

  3. Click on the gear icon ⚙️ next to the interpreter dropdown.

  4. Select Add... from the menu, as shown in the screenshot below.

Since there is no interpreter to add to this screenshot, we must do it from the 'Add Interpreter' menu. 

We have already covered the fact that Python 3.10 and Python 3.8 are both supported by Ubuntu 22.04. Therefore, set up the interpreter to use Python 3.10.

Step 12: Add Project configuration in Pycharm

 

Go to - Current File> Edit Configurations

  1. Click the + (Add) button located in the upper-left corner of the window.

  2. From the list of available templates, select Python.

Once selected, fill in the required fields as shown in the screenshot:

Name: you can provide any name to identify the configuration.

Script Path:

Select the odoo-bin file from the odoo16 directory (not odoo15, if you're working with Odoo 16). This is the main entry point for running the Odoo server.

 

Parameters:

You can specify the parameters required to launch Odoo here. At minimum, provide the path to your configuration file using the -c option:

 

Python Interpreter:

This field should already be populated with the interpreter you configured in the previous step. If not, manually select the correct Python 3 interpreter associated with your project

Step 13: Test Run Odoo 16

 

With all configurations in place, you can now test your setup.
Click the Run ▶️ button in the top-right corner of PyCharm. If everything is configured correctly, the Odoo server should start, and you’ll see logs in the console indicating that the server is running.
You can then open a browser and go to:
http://localhost:8069
If all your configuration was successful, the browser will navigate to the database manager
Odoo as shown below:

Efficiently Setting Up Odoo 16 Development with PyCharm on Ubuntu 22.04

Setting up the Odoo 16 development environment on Ubuntu 22.04 using PyCharm offers a dependable and efficient platform for developing and customizing Odoo modules. With the correct Python setup, essential dependencies, and a structured project configuration, PyCharm is a powerful tool for streamlining and improving your development workflow.

By following the steps outlined, you’re ready to begin developing, debugging, and extending Odoo modules confidently.

Title: How to Set Credit Limit Validation in Odoo POS with JavaScript
Content:
In real-world retail environments—whether you're running a supermarket, a fashion boutique, or a B2B outlet—enforcing customer credit limits is essential. Allowing customers to purchase on credit can benefit business relationships, but without proper checks, it opens the door to financial risk, cash flow issues, and bad debts. While Odoo's backend provides tools to manage credit at the accounting level, the Point of Sale (POS) system, by default, doesn't strictly enforce these credit controls during transactions.

That's where a bit of customization comes into play.

In this blog post, we'll walk you through a technical implementation that enhances the Odoo POS module with credit limit validation. This ensures that credit policies are enforced right at the moment of sale. This solution benefits companies that allow deferred payments or invoice-based transactions from the POS interface.

Step 1: Add Credit Limit Field to Customer Form

First, we ensured the Credit Limit field is Activated from settings .

maximum credit limit per customer.

Step 2:Pass Credit Limit to POS Session (Python Code)

To make this data available in the POS frontend, we inherited the res.partner model and extended the _load_pos_data_fields method:

				
					from odoo import models
class ResPartner(models.Model):
   _inherit = 'res.partner'
   def _load_pos_data_fields(self, config_id):
       data = super()._load_pos_data_fields(config_id)
       data += ['use_partner_credit_limit', 'credit_limit']
       return data

This ensures that both use_partner_credit_limit and credit_limit values are sent to the POS frontend when the session is loaded.

Step 3: Add JavaScript Validation in POS

We patched the POS flow to check if the selected customer's credit limit is exceeded when clicking the Payment button.

				
					import { PosStore } from "@point_of_sale/app/store/pos_store";
import { patch } from "@web/core/utils/patch";
import{AlertDialog }from "@web/core/confirmation_dialog/confirmation_dialog";
import { _t } from "@web/core/l10n/translation";
patch(PosStore.prototype, {
   async pay() {
       const currentOrder = this.get_order();
       if (!currentOrder.canPay()) {
           return;
       }
       const customer = currentOrder.get_partner();
       const total = currentOrder.get_total_with_tax();
       const credit_limit_validation = customer ? customer.is_credit_limit : false;
       // Credit Limit Validation
       if (
           credit_limit_validation &&
           total > customer.credit_limit &&
           pos_credit_limit_validation
       ) {
           this.env.services.dialog.add(AlertDialog, {
               title: _t("Credit Limit Exceeded"),
               body: _t(
                   `The customer's credit limit is ${customer.credit_limit}, but the total order amount is ${total}.nnPlease review the order or get approval before continuing.`
               ),
           });
           return;
       }
       await super.pay();
   }
});

This patch intercepts the payment process and checks if the current order total is greater than the customer's credit limit. If it is, an alert dialog is shown to the cashier preventing the transaction from proceeding.
POS Alert - Credit Limit Exceeded

If the customer's credit limit is lower than the total POS order amount, the system prevents payment and shows an informative message.

Strengthening Credit Control in Odoo POS

This customization improves financial control by implementing customer credit limits directly within the POS interface. By integrating backend logic in Python with real-time JavaScript validations on the front end, businesses can prevent over-crediting at the source. This approach helps maintain healthier cash flow while ensuring that sales operations remain efficient and unobstructed.

Title: What are Computed, Inverse, & Onchange Functions in Odoo?
Content:
Computed, Inverse, and Onchange functions are powerful tools in Odoo that help create dynamic and interactive business applications. These functions allow developers to automate calculations, manage data consistency, and enhance user experience within forms. Computed fields dynamically calculate values based on dependencies, while inverse methods enable users to update these fields manually. Onchange functions in Odoo respond instantly to changes in form fields without saving data. Together, they form the backbone of reactive behavior in Odoo modules.

Computed, Inverse and Onchange Functions in Odoo

When building custom modules in Odoo, you’ll often need to create dynamic fields that automatically calculate values, or update other fields when something changes. Odoo provides powerful tools like @api.depends, @api.onchange, and inverse methods to handle this behavior cleanly.

In this blog, we'll walk you through how to implement these features using a practical use case, managing employee salary details with automatic calculations and dynamic form behavior.

Use Case: Employee Salary Logic

We want to manage employee salary information with the following logic:

  • When a monthly salary is entered, the yearly salary should be automatically calculated.
  • If a user edits the yearly salary, the monthly salary should update too.
  • When the user selects an employee type (e.g., 'Intern', 'Full-time'), the monthly salary should default to a preset value.

Let’s break this down step-by-step.

Compute Field in Odoo

A compute field in Odoo is a field whose value is calculated dynamically based on other fields rather than stored directly in the database (unless you specify store=True). store=True : Caches the value in the database for faster access.

This tells Odoo to cache the computed value in the database, which improves performance and allows the field to be used in search filters and views.

Step 1: Python Model (models/employee_salary.py)

				
					from odoo import models, fields, api
from odoo.exceptions import UserError
class EmployeeSalary(models.Model):
	_name = 'employee.salary'
	_description = 'Employee Salary Info'
	name = fields.Char(string="Employee Name", required=True)
	employee_type = fields.Selection([
    	('intern', 'Intern'),
    	('fulltime', 'Full-time'),
    	('contract', 'Contract')
	], string="Employee Type")
	monthly_salary = fields.Float(string="Monthly Salary")
	yearly_salary = fields.Float(
    	string="Yearly Salary",
    	compute="_compute_yearly_salary",
    	inverse="_inverse_yearly_salary",
    	store=True
	)
	@api.depends('monthly_salary')
	def _compute_yearly_salary(self):
    	for rec in self:
        	rec.yearly_salary = rec.monthly_salary * 12
	def _inverse_yearly_salary(self):
    	for rec in self:
        	rec.monthly_salary = rec.yearly_salary / 12
	@api.onchange('employee_type')
	def _onchange_employee_type_set_salary(self):
    	if self.employee_type == 'intern':
        	self.monthly_salary = 10000
    	elif self.employee_type == 'fulltime':
        	self.monthly_salary = 40000
    	elif self.employee_type == 'contract':
        	self.monthly_salary = 25000

Step 2: XML View

Here’s the corresponding XML file to display the form and list views of the salary model.

				
					
    	employee.salary.form
    	employee.salary
    	employee.salary.tree
    	employee.salary
    	Employee Salaries
    	employee.salary
    	list,form

Understanding the Decorators

@api.depends: 

This tells Odoo that the yearly_salary depends on the value of monthly_salary. So when monthly_salary changes, Odoo recalculates yearly_salary.

Inverse Method in Odoo

Odoo computed fields are usually read-only. But if you want users to edit a computed field manually, you must define an inverse method. This lets Odoo know how to reverse-calculate the dependent field.

In our example:

Editing yearly_salary will update monthly_salary via the _inverse_yearly_salary method.

@api.onchange:

This is used to update field values dynamically in the form view, before saving. Here, we use it to set a default salary based on the selected employee type.

In our case:

When a user selects an employee_type, the system automatically sets a default monthly salary based on the type.

Final Output

Now, when you go to your custom model:

  • Choosing ‘Full-time’ sets the monthly salary to ₹40,000 automatically.
  • Changing the monthly salary auto-calculates the yearly salary instantly.
  • Editing the yearly salary will update the monthly salary.

Using real ORM techniques, you’ve now built a smart, reactive Odoo form!

This demonstrates the power of Odoo’s ORM and decorators to create reactive, smart forms that simplify data entry and reduce human error.

Why These Features Matter

Computed fields, inverse methods, and onchange decorators are essential for every Odoo developer’s toolkit. With them, you can build responsive, user-friendly models that handle data elegantly and reduce errors. By understanding these features, you can:

  • Automate complex calculations.
  • Ensure data consistency across related fields.
  • Improve user experience with dynamic, real-time updates.

If you're building Odoo applications, integrating these decorators into your models will significantly enhance backend efficiency and usability.

Title: What is the OWL Framework in Odoo 18?
Content:
Ever think about how Odoo keeps getting smoother, faster, and more user-friendly with every version? It’s not just about better features - it’s also about the technology behind the scenes. With Odoo 18, something exciting is happening: a modern JavaScript framework called OWL Framework.

Don’t worry if you’re not a tech expert - this blog breaks it down. Whether you're a developer diving into custom Odoo apps or just someone curious about how Odoo builds such innovative interfaces, we’ll walk you through what OWL is, why it matters, and how it’s changing how Odoo looks and feels on the frontend.

The Genesis of OWL: Why Reinvent the Wheel?

Before OWL, Odoo’s frontend was built mainly with QWeb templates and a more imperative JavaScript style. Although functional, this setup had some challenges related to:

  • Complexity
  • Reusability
  • Performance, especially in interactive apps

OWL solved these problems by introducing a component-based, reactive architecture, which is a big shift towards modern frontend engineering. This paradigm shift brought:

  • Improved Modularity: Components are self-contained and reusable
  • Better Maintainability: Localised logic reduces unintended side effects
  • Faster Performance: Thanks to a virtual DOM and optimised updates
  • More Predictable Workflows: Structured code leads to a better developer experience

Core Concepts of the OWL Framework

To truly understand OWL, we need to delve into its key principles:

1. Components: The Building Blocks of UI

At its heart, OWL is all about components. Think of them as the Lego bricks of your user interface. Each component encapsulates its logic (JavaScript code), presentation (XML template), and state.

A basic OWL component in Odoo 18 is typically defined as a JavaScript class that extends owl. Component:

				
					/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { xml } from "@odoo/owl";
export class MyGreeting extends Component {
    static template = xml`
            
Hello, !

    `;
    setup() {
        this.state = useState({ name: "World" });
    }
}

In this simple example:

  • We import necessary modules from @odoo/owl.
  • MyGreeting is our component class.
  • static template defines the component's structure using Odoo's XML template syntax.
  • setup() is a lifecycle hook where we initialise the component's state using the useState hook.

2. Templates: Defining the View

OWL components use XML templates to declare their structure and how data should be rendered. These templates are powerful and offer features like:

  • Data Binding (t-esc):

    Dynamically displays data from the component's state or props. In our example, <t t-esc="state.name"/> will show the current value of state.name.

  • Conditional Rendering (t-if):

    You can show or hide parts of the template according to a condition.

  • List Rendering (t-foreach):

    Enables you to iterate over arrays and render elements for each item.

  • Event Handling (t-on):

    Attaches event listeners to DOM elements, allowing components to react to user interactions.

  • Component Embedding (t-component):

    Renders other OWL components within the current template, facilitating the creation of complex UIS from smaller, reusable parts.

  • Two-Way Binding (t-model):

    Simplifies the process of synchronising input field values with the component's state, as seen in the <input t-model="state.name"/> example.

3. Reactivity: Data Drives the UI

OWL achieves its core strength through its reactivity system. OWL efficiently updates the DOM parts affected by state changes in components. OWL's automatic DOM manipulation system reduces the need for manual DOM updates, resulting in code that is both shorter and contains fewer errors.

The useState hook is the essential component for this reactivity. It establishes a state variable that reacts to changes. OWL automatically re-renders components and their relevant DOM parts whenever you modify the variable.

4. Props: Passing Data Down the Component Tree

Components often need to receive data from their parent components. This is achieved through props (properties). Props are passed as attributes in the template when a parent component renders a child component using <t t-component="ChildComponent" t-props="{ data: parentData }"/>.

While a child component can access and use props, it should treat them as immutable. If a child needs to modify data, it should communicate back to the parent component using events.

5. Lifecycle Hooks: Tapping into Component Stages

OWL provides several lifecycle hooks that allow you to execute or run the code at specific stages of a component's existence:

  • setup():
    Called once when the component is created. It's the ideal place to initialise state, create refs to DOM elements, and set up event listeners.
  • mounted():
    Called after the component has been inserted into the DOM. This is a good place to perform actions that require the component to be part of the live DOM.
  • willUnmount():
    Called just before the element is removed from the DOM. Use this to clean up resources like event listeners or timers.
  • willUpdateProps(nextProps):
    Called before the component receives new props from its parent. You can use this to react to prop changes.
  • updated():
    called after the element was re-rendered due to state or prop changes.

6. Services: Accessing Odoo's Functionality

OWL components often need to interact with Odoo's backend or other system parts. Services, which are globally available objects that provide specific functionalities, such as making RPC calls, displaying notifications, or managing user sessions, facilitate this.

Components can declare their dependencies on services within their setup() method using the useService() hook:

import { Component, useService } from "@odoo/owl";
import { xml } from "@odoo/owl";
export class MyComponentWithService extends Component {
    static template = xml`Result: `;
    setup() {
        this.rpc = useService("rpc");
        this.state = useState({ result: "Loading..." });
        this._fetchData();
    }
    async _fetchData() {
        const data = await this.rpc("/my/backend/endpoint", {});
        this.state.result = data.value;
    }
}

In this example, we use the RPC service to make an asynchronous call to a backend endpoint.

The Benefits of Embracing OWL Framework in Odoo 18

Title: How to Handle Offline Data Storage in Flutter Using Hive?
Content:
Offline data storage is a core feature in most modern apps, especially those built with Flutter. Whether saving user inputs, caching API responses, or building tools without internet access, managing local data efficiently is essential. Hive offers a lightweight, fast, and Dart-native solution for offline storage. It supports secure data handling and works well across mobile, web, and desktop platforms. This guide explains how to handle offline data storage in Flutter using Hive. Ready to level up your Flutter app’s performance even without a connection? Let’s dive in.

Why Local Data Storage Matters in Flutter

Data storage locally is a requirement for almost every app. Whether you want to cache REST API responses, build an application that runs offline, or store customer information for a food delivery app, offline storage is essential.

Flutter offers several local persistence solutions:

shared_preferences: Best for small key-value pairs.

sqflite: Ideal for complex relationships in relational data.

Hive: A fast, secure, lightweight, and Dart-native key-value database—perfect for Flutter Web and offline-first apps.

We’ll explore using Hive in Flutter to perform full offline CRUD operations and build a sample user list app.

Why Hive?

Hive is:

  • Written in pure Dart
  • Blazing fast (benchmarked faster than sqflite)
  • AES-256 encrypted for security
  • Compatible with Flutter Web

How Do You Get Started with Hive in Flutter?

Step 1: Add Dependencies

Add the following to your pubspec.yaml:

				
					dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  hive: ^2.2.3
  hive_flutter: ^1.1.0
dev_dependencies:
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
  hive_generator: ^1.1.3
  build_runner: ^2.2.0

This setup includes the core Hive package and the Flutter extension for UI integration. build_runner and hive_generator are required to generate adapters.

Step 2: Initialize Hive

Initialize Hive in your main.dart before calling runApp():

				
					void main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Hive.initFlutter();
  Hive.registerAdapter(UserModelAdapter());
  await Hive.openBox('userBox');
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

This ensures Hive is ready and the userBox is open for use. Registering the adapter is mandatory for custom object storage.

Step 3: Define the Model and Generate Adapter

Create a new file named user_model.dart and define the model:

				
					import 'package:hive/hive.dart';
part 'user_model.g.dart';
@HiveType(typeId: 0)
class UserModel extends HiveObject {
  @HiveField(0)
  final String name; 
  @HiveField(1)
  final String hobby; 
  @HiveField(2)
  final String description;
  UserModel({
    required this.name,
    required this.hobby,
    required this.description,
  });
}

Now, run this command to generate the adapter:

				
					flutter packages pub run build_runner build

This command creates user_model.g.dart, allowing Hive to serialize and deserialize the model data.

Performing CRUD Operations with Hive

Once Hive is set up, you can perform CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on your data.

1. Add Data

To add a user to the Hive box:

				
					var userBox = Hive.box('users');
userBox.add(User(name: 'Alice', age: 30));

Use the add() method to insert a new entry into the box. Hive will automatically assign the entry a key.

2. Read Data

To retrieve data from the box:

				
					var userBox = Hive.box('users');
User? user = userBox.getAt(0);

Using getAt (), you can retrieve a user by their index. This makes reading values quick and straightforward.

3. Update Data

To update a user's data:

				
					userBox.putAt(0, User(name: 'Alice', age: 31));

Updating a record requires its index. Use putAt() to replace the object at that specific index.

4. Delete Data

To delete a user from the box:

				
					userBox.deleteAt(0);

Use deleteAt() to remove an entry at the given index. The change will be reflected instantly in the UI with ValueListenableBuilder.

Building the UI

Here’s the full UI and logic for the Flutter Hive CRUD App.

File: main.dart

				
					import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:hive_flutter/hive_flutter.dart';
import 'user_model.dart';
void main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Hive.initFlutter();
  Hive.registerAdapter(UserModelAdapter());
  await Hive.openBox('userBox');
  runApp(const MyApp());
}
class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key}); 
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Flutter Hive Database',
      home: UserListScreen(),
    );
  }
}
class UserListScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  final Box box = Hive.box('userBox');
  void showUserDialog(BuildContext context, {UserModel? user, int? index}) {
    final nameController = TextEditingController(text: user?.name);
    final hobbyController = TextEditingController(text: user?.hobby);
    final descController = TextEditingController(text: user?.description);
   showDialog(
      context: context,
      builder: (_) => AlertDialog(
        title: Text(user == null ? 'Add User' : 'Update User'),
        content: Column(
          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
          children: [
            TextField(controller: nameController, decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Name')),
            TextField(controller: hobbyController, decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Hobby')),
            TextField(controller: descController, decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Description')),
          ],
        ),
        actions: [
          TextButton(
            onPressed: () {
              final userModel = UserModel(
                name: nameController.text,
                hobby: hobbyController.text,
                description: descController.text,
              );
              if (user == null) {
                box.add(userModel);
              } else if (index != null) {
                box.putAt(index, userModel);
              }
              Navigator.pop(context);
            },
            child: Text(user == null ? 'Add' : 'Update'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
  void confirmDelete(BuildContext context, int index) {
    final user = box.getAt(index);
    showDialog(
      context: context,
      builder: (_) => AlertDialog(
        title: Text('Are you sure you want to delete ${user?.name}?'),
        actions: [
          TextButton(
            onPressed: () {
              box.deleteAt(index);
              Navigator.pop(context);
            },
            child: const Text('Yes'),
          ),
          TextButton(
            onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context),
            child: const Text('No'),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Flutter Hive Database')),
      body: ValueListenableBuilder(
        valueListenable: box.listenable(),
        builder: (context, Box box, _) {
          return ListView.builder(
            itemCount: box.length,
            itemBuilder: (context, index) {
              final user = box.getAt(index);
              return Card(
                margin: const EdgeInsets.all(8.0),
                child: ListTile(
                  title: Text('${user?.name} | ${user?.description}'),
                  subtitle: Text('Hobby: ${user?.hobby}'),
                  trailing: Row(
                    mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
                    children: [
                      IconButton(
                        icon: const Icon(Icons.edit),
                        onPressed: () => showUserDialog(context, user: user, index: index),
                      ),
                      IconButton(
                        icon: const Icon(Icons.delete),
                        onPressed: () => confirmDelete(context, index),
                      ),
                    ],
                  ),
                ),
              );
            },
          );
        },
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: () => showUserDialog(context),
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}

This UI allows users to add, view, update, and delete records. Thanks to Valuelistenablebuilder, all changes are reflected in real time.

Final Thoughts on Offline Data Storage in Flutter Using Hive

In this tutorial, we learned how to:

  • Setup Hive in a Flutter app
  • Create a TypeAdapter with build_runner
  • Perform full CRUD operations: Add, View, Update, Delete
  • Build a modern UI using ValueListenableBuilder

Hive offers a blazing-fast, secure, and simple solution for local data storage, making it one of the best options for offline-first Flutter apps. Whether targeting mobile, web, or desktop, Hive is an excellent choice for smooth and efficient offline data handling.

If building production-ready apps, consider exploring advanced features like encrypted boxes, lazy boxes, or custom keys. Hive has you covered.

Title: How to Implement Rating Bar in Flutter?
Content:
User feedback is essential in mobile app development - it shapes product improvements, drives user engagement, and ultimately impacts the success of your application. A simple and intuitive method for collecting this feedback is through a rating bar system. In this post, we'll walk through how to create a responsive and customizable Rating Screen in Flutter using the powerful flutter_rating_bar package.

Whether you're building a food delivery app, e-commerce store, or service platform, enabling users to leave ratings can provide you with the insights you need while enhancing their overall experience.

Why Use a Rating Bar in Your App?

A rating bar provides users with a familiar, visual way to assess their experience. It simplifies the feedback process by reducing cognitive effort, making it easier to share opinions quickly. Ratings can:

  • Guide future users with peer insights.
  • Provide quantifiable data for analytics.
  • Help developers understand usability gaps.
  • Improve your app’s credibility and engagement metrics.

Flutter’s flexibility makes it easy to implement visually attractive, feature-rich rating widgets that match your design needs, and with the flutter_rating_bar plugin, the process becomes even simpler.

1. Getting Started

Before jumping into code, let’s get the basics out of the way. Follow these steps to create a new Flutter project:

  • Open Android Studio or VS Code.
  • Go to File > New > New Flutter Project.
  • Name your project (e.g., flutter_rating_app).
  • Select the Flutter SDK path and finish the setup.

To test the app, launch a Test Device:

  • Click Create Device in the left panel.
  • Choose a device type and launch it.

2. Add Required Dependencies

To use the flutter_rating_bar package, you’ll need to add it to your ubspec.yaml file:

				
					dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  flutter_rating_bar: ^4.0.0

Run the following command to install the dependency:

				
					flutter pub get

This command fetches the package and makes it available in your app.

3. Import Packages

At the top of your Dart file, import the necessary libraries:

				
					import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_rating_bar/flutter_rating_bar.dart';

4. Build the Rating Screen

4.1 Create the Screen

Let’s build a stateful widget to handle dynamic updates when a user interacts with the rating bar.

				
					class RatingBarScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  @override
  _RatingBarState createState() => _RatingBarState();
}

4.2 Define the State Class

				
					class _RatingBarState extends State<RatingBarScreen> {
  double value = 3.5;
  double _userRating = 3.0;
  IconData? _selectedIcon;
  TextEditingController _ratingController = TextEditingController();
  bool _isVertical = false;
  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _ratingController = TextEditingController(text: '3.0');
  }

Here, we're initialising the rating controller and updating it dynamically as the user interacts with the rating bar.

5. Build the UI

Now it’s time to design the screen layout and plug in our rating bar.

5.1 Scaffold and Layout

				
					
 @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: Text('Rating Screen'),
      ),
      body: Padding(
        padding: EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16.0),
        child: Column(
          mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center,
          children: [
            Text("Rate our service"),
            SizedBox(height: 10),
            RatingBar.builder(
              initialRating: 2,
              minRating: 1,
              direction: Axis.horizontal,
              allowHalfRating: true,
              itemCount: 5,
              itemBuilder: (context, _) => Icon(
                Icons.star,
                color: Colors.amber,
              ),
              onRatingUpdate: (rating) {
                print("User rated: $rating");
              },
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

The user sees a set of stars to rate the service, and the numeric rating updates in a read-only text field.

6. Customize Your Rating Bar

You can also fully customize the icons using RatingWidget:

				
					RatingBar(
  ratingWidget: RatingWidget(
    full: Icon(Icons.star, color: Colors.green),
    half: Icon(Icons.star_half, color: Colors.green),
    empty: Icon(Icons.star_border, color: Colors.green),
  ),
  onRatingUpdate: (rating) => print("Rated: $rating"),
  itemSize: 40,
  initialRating: 4.5,
  itemCount: 5,
)

This adds your personality to the app, whether you use hearts, stars, emojis, or custom icons.

8. Output

The output is a sleek UI with a row of stars that users can tap to give feedback. It’s smooth, visually appealing, and easy to interact with.

9. Bonus Features to Enhance UX

Consider going beyond basic functionality. Here are a few bonus features to add polish:

  •  Add a Text Field for comments.

Allow users to explain their rating:

				
					TextField(
  decoration: InputDecoration(
    labelText: 'Leave a comment',
    border: OutlineInputBorder(),
  ),
  maxLines: 3,
),
  •  Integrate with Firebase Firestore or REST API to store and analyze user feedback.
  •  Use Animations for star glow or bounce.
  •  Vertical Layout: Change direction to Axis.vertical.

10. Real-World Use Cases

  • E-commerce apps: Let users rate products.
  • Service platforms: Ask users to rate after service completion.
  • Food delivery apps: Rate food quality, packaging, and delivery.
  • Learning apps: Rate course content or instructors.

Implementing a rating system in Flutter

Implementing a rating system in Flutter doesn’t have to be complicated. With the flutter_rating_bar package, it’s quick, elegant, and highly customizable. Whether you want simple star ratings or a full-blown feedback system with comments and analytics, this package provides a solid foundation.

This feature isn’t just eye candy, it’s a critical UX tool. It makes users feel heard and gives you valuable insights to improve your app.

So go ahead, add that rating screen. Your users (and your future self) will thank you!

Title: How to Configure Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory?
Content:
Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory

Warehouse management has always been challenging, especially when dealing with large orders. With Odoo ERP 18, businesses can facilitate and upgrade their warehouse operations with Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory. This feature allows warehouse workers to update the process, pick multiple orders simultaneously, and significantly reduce picking time.

This detailed guide will walk you through

  • The steps to configure Odoo cluster picking effectively.
  • Explore Odoo 18 inventory picking methods.
  • Odoo 18 batch picking setup.  
  • Key features like Odoo warehouse management.
  • Odoo 18 multi-step routes work together to make your warehouse more efficient.

Understanding how to use Odoo 18 cluster picking configuration will entrust you to speed up order fulfillment, reduce errors, and optimize your warehouse operations.

Let's read!

What Is Odoo 18 Inventory Picking Methods

At its core, Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory is a technique that allows you to pick products for multiple orders in a single task rather than picking one order at a time. This method is particularly useful when fulfilling multiple orders that contain the same items. It is the time workers spend moving around the warehouse, as they can pick everything up in one go.

Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory enables the worker to select all the required quantities for those orders in one trip; for example, if multiple customers or orders require the same product, instead of walking back and forth to pick each item individually, you can pick them at once. This not only speeds up the picking process but also increases the efficiency of warehouse space utilization.

You set up your system to group orders together; configuring Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory can also improve overall warehouse productivity and allow crew or employees to work more efficiently.

Benefits of Using Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory

Understanding the advantages of Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory is important to appreciate its role in warehouse management.

Below are some key benefits:

1. Improve the Efficiency of Warehouse

Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory can significantly enhance warehouse efficiency. By picking products simultaneously for multiple orders, warehouse staff can complete tasks faster, cutting picking times and improving workflow.

2. Reduce Errors

Warehouse workers picking items simultaneously reduces the chances of making mistakes by employing Odoo inventory-picking methods like cluster picking. Items are grouped and selected based on clear pre-defined instructions to minimize any chances of selecting incorrect items.

3. Enhanced Order Fulfilment Speed

Cluster picking speeds up order fulfilment as items can be packed together and shipped more rapidly, meeting customer expectations faster and ensuring orders arrive on time in today's highly competitive e-commerce environment.

4. Cost Savings

Faster and more efficient picking processes directly translate into cost savings. Since Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory reduces the time spent on each order, your warehouse staff can fulfill more orders in less time, allowing you to handle a higher volume without increasing your workforce.

How to Set Up Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory

Setting up Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory requires careful planning and configuration. Let’s take a step-by-step approach.

Step 1: Odoo 18 Batch Picking Setu

Before configuring cluster picking, upgrade your Odoo storage locations configuration:

For this first go to Settings.

And, Enable “packages” and “ batch, waves & cluster transfers” then click on Save.

Enabling Odoo batch picking can further optimize the picking process, especially when combined with Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory.

Also, Enable the storage locations and multi-step routes from settings and save.

Step 2: Enable Cluster Picking

We assign each product a different shelf in the location.

Step 3: Configure Your Warehouse Locations

Organizing your warehouse effectively is essential to ensure that Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory works greatly. Odoo warehouse management allows you to set up different locations within the warehouse. For example:

  • Incoming Shipments: A place or space where new stock arrives.
  • Picking Locations: Where items are picked from for orders.
  • Packing Locations: A place to pack the picked items.
  • Shipping Locations: Where orders are staged before being shipped.

To configure these, go to Inventory > Configuration > warehouses and create the necessary warehouse locations. This step is vital for making the picking process efficient.

Step 4: Odoo 18 multi-step routes

With Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory, setting up Odoo 18 multi-step routes is important. Multi-step routes help define how products are moved through the warehouse, from picking to packing to shipping.

  • Create or edit a route that best suits your picking and delivery process.
  • Assign the route to your warehouse, ensuring that all products follow the optimal path from start to finish.

Using multi-step routes, combined with Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory, ensures a smooth flow of goods through your warehouse, reducing unnecessary delays.

Step 5: Use the Odoo 18 Packages Feature

The Odoo packages feature allows you to group products into packages, which can help speed up the packing process. Once your items are picked using Cluster Picking in Odoo Inventory, you can pack them into packages, making shipping faster and more efficient.

  • Go to Inventory > Products > Packages.

  • Assign items to packages during the packing process.

This feature reduces packing errors and ensures all products are correctly grouped before shipment.

Best Practices for Using Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory

Now that you know how to configure Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory, here are some best practices to make the most out of this feature:

1. Regularly Review Picking Routes

Since your warehouse will likely grow over time, reviewing and adjusting your picking routes regularly is important. Check for bottlenecks or areas that can be optimized for faster picking.

2. Train Your Staff

To maximize Cluster Picking efficiency with Odoo 18 Inventory, ensure your warehouse staff is well-trained in its use. This should include understanding multi-step routes, batch picking, and package features within Odoo.

3. Monitor Performance

Use Odoo’s reporting tools to monitor warehouse performance. Check metrics like picking speed, order fulfillment accuracy, and inventory levels to identify areas for improvement.

Why Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory is Essential for Your Warehouse

Configuring Cluster Picking in Odoo 18 Inventory can significantly facilitate your warehouse operations. By taking advantage of features like warehouse management, batch picking, multi-step routes, and order fulfillment speed improvements, you can increase picking efficiency while decreasing errors and speed. Integrating Odoo storage locations and packages further enhances this process for improved productivity within your warehouse.

By taking advantage of these features and best practices, you can significantly cut regular or operational costs, enhance customer satisfaction, and scale warehouse operations more easily.

Title: How to Implement Barcode & QR Code Scanning in Odoo Apps Using Flutter?
Content:
Barcode and QR Code Scanning in Odoo Apps using Flutter

Barcode and QR code scanning are essential for inventory management, POS systems, and logistics applications. Imagine walking through a warehouse, pointing your phone at a barcode, and instantly updating your inventory in Odoo, no paperwork, no manual entry, just smooth, automated precision. That’s the advantage of combining Flutter’s sleek mobile framework with Odoo’s powerful backend system. In today’s fast-moving business world, speed and accuracy aren’t just goals, they’re essentials. Barcode and QR code scanning bring new efficiency to POS systems, logistics, and inventory tracking. You get real-time updates and more intelligent workflows with just a quick scan. This guide will walk you through building a Flutter app that connects directly with Odoo and transforms how you manage operations.

Prerequisites

  • Flutter installed
  • Odoo backend with necessary modules (Inventory, POS, or custom module for barcode scanning)
  • API access to Odoo (REST or XML-RPC)
  • flutter_barcode_scanner package for scanning

How to Implement Barcode and QR Code Scanning in Odoo Apps Using Flutter: A Step-by-Step Guide

Step 1: Install Dependencies

Add the required package in pubspec.yaml:

				
					dependencies: flutter:
sdk: flutter
flutter_barcode scanner: ^2.0.0 
http: ^0.13.0

Then Run:

				
					flutter pub get

Step 2: Implement Barcode/QR Scanner in Flutter

In this step, you’ll integrate the barcode and QR code scanning feature using the flutter_barcode_scanner package. The scanned data will be captured and displayed within the app's UI for further processing.

				
					class _BarcodeScannerScreenState extends State {
  String _scannedBarcode = '';
  Future scanBarcode() async {
    String barcodeScanResult;
    try {
      barcodeScanResult = await FlutterBarcodeScanner.scanBarcode(
        '#ff6666', 'Cancel', true, ScanMode.BARCODE);
    } catch (e) {
      barcodeScanResult = 'Failed to get barcode';
    }
    setState(() {
      _scannedBarcode = barcodeScanResult;
    });
  }
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text('Scan Barcode/QR Code')),
      body: Center(
        child: Column(
          mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center,
          children: [
            Text('Scanned Code: $_scannedBarcode'),
            ElevatedButton(
              onPressed: scanBarcode,
              child: Text('Scan'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Step 3: Sending Scanned Data to Odoo

Once a barcode is scanned, we need to send the data to Odoo using its API. Below is an example using the Odoo REST API.

				
					import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
import 'dart:convert';
Future sendBarcodeToOdoo(String barcode) async {
  final String url = 'https://your-odoo-instance.com/api/inventory/barcode';
  final response = await http.post(
    Uri.parse(url),
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_ODOO_ACCESS_TOKEN',
    },
    body: jsonEncode({'barcode': barcode}),
  );
  if (response.statusCode == 200) {
    print('Barcode sent successfully');
  } else {
    print('Failed to send barcode: ${response.body}');
  }
}

Call this function after scanning the barcode:

				
					scanBarcode() async {
  String barcodeScanResult = await FlutterBarcodeScanner.scanBarcode(
    '#ff6666',
    'zCancel',
    true,
    ScanMode.BARCODE
  );
  setState(() {
    _scannedBarcode = barcodeScanResult;
  });
  await sendBarcodeToOdoo(_scannedBarcode);
}

Step 4: Handling Odoo Response

Odoo might return inventory details for a scanned product. Parse and display this data in your Flutter app:

				
					Future getProductDetails(String barcode) async {
  final response = await http.get(
    Uri.parse('https://your-odoo-instance.com/api/product?barcode=$barcode'),
    headers: {'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_ODOO_ACCESS_TOKEN'},
  );
  if (response.statusCode == 200) {
    final productData = jsonDecode(response.body);
    print('Product Name: ${productData["name"]}');
  } else {
    print('Product not found');
  }
}

Call this function after scanning:

				
					await getProductDetalis(_scannedBarcode);

Step 5: Displaying Scanned Data in UI

Modify your UI to show product details fetched from Odoo:

				
					Text('Product Name: ${productData["name"]}'),
Text('Stock Quantity: ${productData["quantity"]}'),

Step 6: Error Handling and Edge Cases

To make your application robust, consider handling the following cases:

No Barcode Scanned: Show an error message if the user cancels scanning.

Invalid Barcode: Validate the barcode before sending it to Odoo.

Network Errors: Handle API failures and show appropriate messages.

Odoo Authentication Issues: Implement token expiration handling.

Example:
				
					if (response.statusCode == 401) {
  print('Authentication error. Please log in again.');    
  }

Step 7: Testing the Integration

Before deploying, thoroughly test the barcode scanning functionality:

  1. Test scanning with different barcode types (EAN, UPC, QR, etc.).
  2. Validate API responses and ensure data is correctly fetched from Odoo.
  3. Check UI responsiveness and error handling.
  4. Simulate network failures to test offline handling.

Step 8: Deploying the App

Once testing is complete:

  • Build the Flutter app (flutter build apk or flutter build ios).
  • Deploy the app to Google Play Store or App Store.
  • Ensure Odoo is properly configured to handle barcode requests.

Bringing Smart Scanning to Life with Flutter and Odoo

This guide demonstrates implementing barcode/QR code scanning in Flutter and syncing scanned data with an Odoo backend. By integrating these steps, you can efficiently build inventory management, POS, and logistics applications. Whether aiming for faster checkouts, accurate stock tracking, or simplified warehouse operations, combining Flutter’s flexibility with Odoo’s backend power equips your business with a modern, tech-driven solution.

Title: Odoo ERP vs. Standalone e-Invoicing Tools: What’s Best for ZATCA Compliance?
Content:
Understanding ZATCA Compliance & Why It Matters

When it comes to ZATCA Compliance, every business operating in Saudi Arabia must align with the e-invoicing regulations introduced by the Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA). As companies prepare for Zakat, Tax and Customs AuthorityPhase 2 requirements, many evaluate whether to integrate an ERP like Odoo or use standalone e-invoicing tools.

Whether you're a small business or a growing enterprise, choosing the right Zakat, Tax and Customs Authoritye-invoicing solution can impact your operations, compliance, and costs. This blog explores the differences between Odoo ZATCA- compliance and standalone software and how they each meet ZATCA compliant ERP standards.

With Odoo's seamless e-invoicing integration and all-in-one business management, you might discover the more innovative way to ensure compliance.

What is ZATCA Compliance and Who Needs It?

ZATCA-Compliance refers to the regulatory framework introduced by Saudi Arabia's tax authority that mandates electronic invoicing for all taxable transactions. The system, rolled out in phases, began with Phase 1 in December 2021 and is now transitioning to Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority Phase 2 requirements, which involve more advanced integration with the ZATCA platform.

Businesses must generate invoices in a specific format, incorporate QR codes, include mandatory fields, and ensure secure audit archival. With real-time submission and integration expected in Phase 2, choosing the right tool is critical.

All VAT-registered businesses in Saudi Arabia are required to implement Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority e-invoicing to avoid penalties. Businesses are expected to generate, store, and share invoices electronically in real time, making robust software essential.

Standalone e-Invoicing Tools: Pros and Cons

Advantages of Standalone e-Invoicing Tools

Standalone e-invoicing software in Saudi Arabia offers basic features like invoice generation, QR code inclusion, and secure digital signatures. These tools are often cloud-based and require minimal setup.

  • Fast to deploy
  • Affordable for small businesses
  • Designed solely for ZATCA-compliance
  • Ideal for companies with limited invoicing needs

Disadvantages of Standalone Solutions

While standalone ZATCA e-invoicing tools do the job, they often lack the broader capabilities of a complete Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority-compliant ERP system:

  • No integration with inventory or accounting systems
  • Data has to be entered manually in multiple platforms
  • Difficult to scale operations
  • Limited automation features
  • Often need other tools for reporting and analysis

Why Odoo is the Best ZATCA Compliant ERP Solution

Odoo is a modular, open-source ERP offering comprehensive ZATCA-Compliance support. It handles everything from CRM and inventory to accounting and HR, all integrated with its powerful Odoo e-invoicing integration.

Advantages of Using Odoo for ZATCA Compliance

  • Complete automation of invoice generation based on transactions
  • Real-time validation with Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority servers
  • Seamless handling of QR codes and digital signatures
  • Robust security, traceability, and audit trails
  • Scalable and customizable to fit any industry
  • Proactively updated for compliance with Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority Phase 2 requirements

Odoo's advantage lies in its ability to connect every business process, meaning invoices are generated from real-time, synced business data - sales, stock, payments, all linked in one platform.

In-Depth Comparison: Odoo ERP vs. Standalone e-Invoicing Tools

Here's a realistic comparison table that provides human-readable clarity on how these solutions stack up:

Feature

Standalone e-Invoicing Tool

Odoo ERP with ZATCA Compliance

Initial Setup

Quick, simple, minimal configuration

Requires setup but customizable

Cost Efficiency (long-term)

Lower at start, higher over time

Higher initially, better ROI

ZATCA Phase 2 Readiness

Basic support, may need updates

Fully integrated and compliant

Integration with Other Modules

None

Fully integrated with CRM, HR, etc.

Setting Up Vendor Price List in Odoo 18

Accessing Vendor Price List Configuration

To begin managing vendor price list in Odoo 18, navigate to the Purchase module:​

  • Purchase > Configuration > Vendor Price Lists​

Here, you can view existing price lists or create new ones tailored to specific vendors.

Creating a New Vendor Price List

 

To create a new vendor price list: Click on Create.

  1. Select the Vendor for whom the pricelist is intended.

  2. Define the Product and specify the Unit Price.

  3. Optionally, set a Discount percentage and Delivery Lead Time.

        4.  Save the pricelist.​

This setup ensures that when creating purchase orders or requests for quotations, Odoo automatically applies the defined terms, streamlining the procurement process.​

Importing Vendor Price List in Odoo 18

For businesses with extensive vendor lists, manually entering pricelist data can be time-consuming. Odoo 18 facilitates bulk import of vendor price lists via CSV or XLSX files.​

Title: How Can Beginners Build a Scalable Flutter Architecture?
Content:
Building a scalable Flutter architecture might sound intimidating for beginners, but it’s the secret to crafting apps that grow smoothly with your ambitions. Instead of rushing into code, understanding the proper structure can save hours of rework later. Flutter’s flexibility allows you to design smart, efficient apps, but only if you set strong foundations early. With the right approach, you can avoid messy codebases and future frustrations. In this guide, we'll break down the essentials in a clear, practical, and beginner-friendly way. Whether building your first project or planning ahead, you’re in the right place. So, let’s dive in and discover the true potential of Flutter development!

Building a Scalable Flutter Architecture: A Guide for Beginners

Flutter is an excellent framework. It helps us build excellent mobile apps very easily. For small-scale apps, we don't need to consider the architecture, but in the case of large-scale apps, this architecture helps us very much. That's why these architectures are important.

Why is Architecture Important?

A well-structured architecture:

  • Improves code readability and maintainability
  • Enhances scalability and facilitates team collaboration
  • Ensures smooth integration of new features and updates

Common Architecture Patterns in Flutter

Several architectural patterns are commonly used in Flutter. Here’s a quick look at the main ones:

1. MVC (Model-View-Controller)

  • Model: Handles data and business logic
  • View: Displays UI components
  • Controller: Manages user input and updates Model & View

Use Case: MVC is a good choice for small projects. However, it’s not the best option regarding scalability and handling complex applications.

2. MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel)

  • Model: Manages the application data
  • View: Displays UI and listens to ViewModel changes
  • ViewModel: Acts as a bridge between Model and View

Use Case: MVVM works well with state management libraries like Provider or Riverpod, making it an excellent choice for apps requiring a moderate scalability level.

3. Clean Architecture (Recommended for Scalability)

Clean Architecture divides the app into distinct layers:

  • Presentation Layer (UI + State Management)
  • Domain Layer (Business Logic)
  • Data Layer (API, Local Database, Repositories)

Use Case: Clean Architecture is best suited for large and complex applications with priorities for scalability, testing, and maintenance.

Setting Up a Scalable Flutter Architecture

Once you understand the importance of architecture, the next step is setting up your project correctly.

1. Project Structure

Organize your Flutter project clearly and logically. Here's a recommended folder structure:

This separation ensures that different concerns (UI, business logic, data management) remain isolated and manageable.

2. Implementing State Management

Choosing the right state management solution is key to scalability. Popular options include:

  • Provider: Simple and effective for medium-sized apps
  • GetX: Lightweight and great for handling dependencies
  • Bloc (Business Logic Component): Best suited for large applications that require complex state transitions and robust event handling.

Selecting the right tool depends on the complexity and size of your app.

Best Practices for Building a Scalable Flutter Architecture

When building a scalable Flutter architecture, following best practices is essential to ensure your app is maintainable, performant, and adaptable to changes. Here are some recommended best practices:

1. Keep Business Logic Separate

One of the most essential principles in scalable architecture is separating business logic from the UI. This reduces the UI's complexity and allows for easier testing and maintenance. Use architecture patterns like Clean Architecture or MVVM to ensure business logic is isolated in the Domain Layer, separate from UI components.

2. Use Dependency Injection

Use a dependency injection (DI) framework like GetIt or Riverpod to manage dependencies efficiently and reduce tight coupling. DI ensures that your components remain modular and testable. It also helps when switching to different services (e.g., API calls and databases) without affecting the rest of the app.

3. Prioritize State Management

State management is a crucial part of scalable architecture. Flutter offers several state management approaches, including Provider, Riverpod, GetX, and Bloc. Choose one based on your project's complexity to ensure the state management is predictable, scalable, and easy to test.

4. Follow SOLID Principles

SOLID is a set of five principles that guide object-oriented design and software development. Following these principles ensures that your code is modular, reusable, and easy to maintain. Here's a quick overview of the SOLID principles:

  • S: Single Responsibility Principle
  • O: Open/Closed Principle
  • L: Liskov Substitution Principle
  • I: Interface Segregation Principle
  • D: Dependency Inversion Principle

5. Ensure Proper Error Handling and Logging

When scaling up your app, you'll encounter various exceptions and errors. Proper error handling ensures your app remains stable, even in unexpected conditions. Additionally, a logging system should be integrated to track issues, which helps debug and maintain the app as it grows.

6. Leverage Modularization

Modularization refers to splitting your application into smaller, independent modules or packages. This allows teams to work on different parts of the app without stepping on each other's toes and also helps reduce build times. Flutter's packages and plugins make breaking down the app into reusable components easier.

Building a Strong Foundation for Future Growth

As a beginner, investing time in understanding and applying scalable Flutter architecture can save you countless hours in the future. Whether you start small with MVC, level up with MVVM, or adopt a completely Clean Architecture for larger projects, the proper structure will make your development process smoother, faster, and more professional. Remember, strong architecture isn't just about clean code; it's about building apps ready for growth.
