Title: How to Create Rainbow Man Effect & Display Notifications in Odoo 18?
Content:
Why User Experience in Odoo Matters

Looking to make your Odoo environment more interactive and user-friendly? One of the easiest yet most valuable ways to enhance user experience in Odoo is to incorporate visual feedback mechanisms like the Rainbow Effect and Display Notifications.

These playful yet powerful features bring a sense of achievement to everyday tasks and help users stay informed and motivated. Whether you're managing sales, completing assignments, or confirming actions, these subtle touches can turn routine processes into satisfying moments.

Odoo is more than just a powerful ERP system; it also comes packed with thoughtful UX enhancements that make user interaction smoother and more engaging. Two such features are the Rainbow Effect and Display Notifications. These enhancements visually confirm user actions and highlight completed processes in a fun, dynamic way.

In this blog, we'll walk you through:

  • How to add a Rainbow Effect by inheriting the sale.order.model.
  • How to implement a Display Notification by inheriting the purchase.order.model.

What is the Rainbow Effect in Odoo?

The Rainbow Effect in Odoo is a UI animation that appears as a reward when an action is completed, like confirming a sale order. This effect not only delights users but also gives them a sense of accomplishment.

This feature is handy for sales teams, providing instant positive feedback for closing deals or confirming orders. Here's how you can implement it:

Add Rainbow Effect to Sale Order Confirmation

				
					from odoo import fields,api,models
from odoo.exceptions import ValidationError
class SaleOrder(models.Model):
   _inherit = 'sale.order'
def action_confirm(self):
   super(SaleOrder, self).action_confirm()
   return {
       'effect': {
           'fadeout': 'slow',
           'message': 'Sale order is confirmed',
           'type': 'rainbow_man',
       }
   }

Explanation:

  • The fadeout effect can be adjusted to either a fast or slow transition.
  • The Message refers to the text displayed alongside the rainbow_man effect. 

After confirming the sale order, an effect appears on the displayed message.

What is Display Notification in Odoo?

Display Notification in Odoo is a toast-style message shown to the user after an action is triggered. It provides instant feedback, for example, confirming that a record was successfully saved or a process was completed. Here's how you can add this to a purchase order confirmation:

Add Display Notification to Purchase Order Confirmation

				
					from odoo import models
class PurchaseOrder(models.Model):
   _inherit = 'purchase.order'
def button_confirm(self):
   res = super().button_confirm()
   return {
       'type': 'ir.actions.client',
       'tag': 'display_notification',
       'params': {
           'title': 'Confirmed',
           'message': 'Purchase Order Confirmed Successfully! ✅',
           'type': 'success',  # 'success', 'warning', 'danger', 'info'
           'sticky': False,
       }
   }

Explanation:

  • The title of the notification box.
  • The message content is displayed to the user.
  • Controls the style of the notification (e.g., success, warning, danger, info).
  • If True, the Message stays on screen until dismissed manually. If False, it disappears automatically.

This notification confirms the action to the user and improves transparency in system operations without adding friction to the workflow.

The screenshot below shows a toast message at the top of the screen when a Purchase Order is confirmed, indicating that the action was successful.

Finishing Strong with User Delight

Title: How to Post Messages to Chatter in Odoo 18?
Content:
Posting Messages to Chatter in Odoo 18

Odoo is well known for integrating business processes, from sales and CRM to inventory and project management. One of its lesser-celebrated but compelling features is Chatter, a communication tool embedded within most Odoo models.

Whether you're tracking a deal in CRM, moving tasks across stages in a project, or reviewing an invoice, Chatter helps your team stay in the loop. With every change logged and visible, communication becomes contextual and traceable.

In Chatter in Odoo 18, it plays a key role in driving collaboration. But what if you want to post messages to Chatter automatically, without manual input? In this blog, we’ll walk you through exactly how to do that, using a custom example, and explain why this feature is a valuable part of your development toolkit.

What is Chatter in Odoo 18?

Before discussing the technical aspects, let’s briefly explain Chatter and its usefulness.

Chatter is Odoo’s built-in messaging and activity tracking system. It appears as a threaded communication log on most form views, showing:

  • System-generated logs (like stage changes or status updates)
  • Manual user messages and comments
  • Scheduled activities
  • Email threads
  • File attachments

This creates a centralised history of interactions and changes for each record. It’s beneficial for teams working remotely or across departments.

Why Post Messages to Chatter Programmatically?

There are many scenarios where you might want to post messages automatically using code:

  • Automated workflows: Notify stakeholders when a task progresses without manual input.
  • Custom buttons: Trigger communication on specific user actions like approving a quote or updating a course status.
  • Reminders and updates: Push alerts based on time triggers or business conditions.
  • Status tracking: Log state transitions, like moving from “draft” to “approved.”

This improves transparency and ensures key updates don’t go unnoticed.

How to Post a Message to Chatter in Odoo 18

We create a model student, for instance, to keep track of a student’s course status (such as “draft,” “in_progress,” or “completed”). When users click the “Start Course” or “Complete Course” buttons, the course status and a message are immediately sent to the chatter to inform them of the change.

  • start_course method: This method sends a message stating that the course has begun and changes the state to “in_progress”.
  • _course method: Sends a message stating that the course changes the status to “completed”.

This tweak makes sure that everyone is notified whenever the course status changes by posting a notice in the discussion.

To add the feature where you post a message to the relevant student in Odoo 18 when the course status changes (using self.message_post()), here's how you can modify your model and methods to support the functionality as you described.

Key Steps:

  1. Post the message to the student’s Chatter (using self.message_post()).
  2. Customise the message with HTML content, attachments, and email (if required).
  3. Track the conversation between the student and the course updates.

Below is a detailed approach with the necessary changes for posting a message in Chatter when the course status changes, with all the specifications you mentioned.

				
					Updated Model Definition with message_post()
from odoo import models, fields, api
from odoo.tools import html2plaintext
class Student(models.Model):
	_name = 'academy.student'
	_inherit = ['mail.thread', 'mail.activity.mixin']  	   _description = 'Student'
	name = fields.Char(string='Student Name', required=True, tracking=True)
	course_state = fields.Selection([
    	('draft', 'Draft'),
    	('in_progress', 'In Progress'),
    	('completed', 'Completed')
	], default='draft', string='Course Status', tracking=True)
	def start_course(self):
    	for rec in self:
         	rec.course_state = 'in_progress
         	message_body = f"📘 Course started for <b>{rec.name}</b>."
        	rec.message_post(
            	body=message_body,
            	message_type='notification',
            	subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note',
            	partner_ids=[rec.user_id.partner_id.id],            	         body_is_html=True	)
        	# Optionally, send an email notification (if you want to notify via email)
        	rec.message_post(
            	body=f"Course has started for {rec.name}.",
            	message_type='email',
            	email_from=self.env.user.email,
            	subject="Course Started"
        	)
	def complete_course(self):
    	for rec in self:
        	rec.course_state = 'completed'
        	message_body = f"🎓 Course completed for <b>{rec.name}</b>."
        	rec.message_post(
            	body=message_body,
            	message_type='notification',
            	subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note',
            	partner_ids=[rec.user_id.partner_id.id],  
            	body_is_html=True  # Allow HTML content
        	)
        	# Optionally, send an email notification
        	rec.message_post(
            	body=f"The course has been completed for {rec.name}.",
            	message_type='email',
            	email_from=self.env.user.email,
            	subject="Course Completed"
        	)

Button Configuration in the Form View (XML)

You can create Start Course and Complete Course buttons in the student form view. These buttons will trigger the start_course() and complete_course() methods.

				
					<record id="view_form_student" model="ir.ui.view">
	<field name="name">academy.student.form</field>
	<field name="model">academy.student</field>
	<field name="arch" type="xml">
    	<form string="Student">
<header>
    <button name="start_course" type="object" string="Start Course" invisible = “course_state != 'draft'"/>
	<button name="complete_course" type="object" string="Complete Course" invisible = “course_state != 'in_progress'"/>
<field name="course_state" widget = “statusbar” statusbar_visible=”draft,in_progress,completed” />
	</header>
        	<sheet>
            	<group>
                	<field name="name"/>
             	</group>
            	        	</sheet>
 				<chatter/>
        	    	</form>
	</field>
</record>

Graphical View of the Student Model Chatter Section

Understanding message_post() Parameters

Here’s a quick breakdown of useful arguments in the message_post() method.

Parameter

Description

body

The message body (can be plain text or HTML).

body_is_html

Set to True to allow HTML formatting.

message_type

Use 'notification' for internal logs or 'email' for external emails.

subtype_xmlid

Defines the subtype; 'mail.mt_note' is common for logs.

partner_ids

Send message to specific users (optional).

subject

Subject line when sending as an email.

email_from

Sender address (usually from self.env.user.email).

Benefits of Using Chatter in Odoo 18 for Status Updates

Why go through the trouble of integrating message_post() in your models?

Here’s what you gain:

  • Automated communication: Reduce manual steps while keeping the team informed.
  • Full traceability: Every state change and action is logged with a timestamp and user ID.
  • Improved UX: Users can scroll through the Chatter to get the full history of a record.
  • Integrated collaboration: Combine messages, activities, and attachments in one unified interface.

This kind of automation ensures that no important update slips through the cracks, especially in multi-user systems or team-based workflows.

Keep your team informed.

Integrating Chatter in Odoo 18 significantly enhances collaboration and traceability by allowing users to log changes, share updates, and schedule activities directly within a record. In this blog, we discussed how to post messages to Chatter when a student's course status changes, using the message_post() method with dynamic content.

By inheriting mail.thread and mail.activity.mixin in our custom model and including the <chatter/> section correctly in the form view (outside the <sheet> tag), we ensure the Chatter renders correctly and functions as expected. This setup allows team members to stay informed about important events like the start or completion of a course, improving transparency and efficiency.

Title: What is Error Management in Odoo?
Content:
Understanding Error Management in Odoo

Error Management in Odoo: Errors are inevitable in software development. How well a system handles those errors sets a great system apart from a mediocre one. For developers working with Odoo, understanding how to manage exceptions properly is essential for debugging and maintaining a smooth and intuitive user experience.

Odoo, known for its modular and user-centric design, offers a robust error-handling system. At the heart of this system is the Odoo Exceptions Module, which defines several core exception types that interact seamlessly with the framework's Remote Procedure Call (RPC) layer.

This blog explores these core exceptions, their purpose, real-life use cases, and why they are essential for developing stable and user-friendly applications.

Why Exception Handling Matters in Odoo

Before getting into the individual exceptions, it's essential to understand the bigger picture.

When an error occurs and the RPC layer does not correctly recognise it, Odoo will respond with a generic "Server Error" message. This confuses end users and makes it harder for developers to troubleshoot the issue. That’s where these well-defined exceptions come in. They allow for clear communication between the backend and front end, offering specific feedback that can be addressed more easily.

Let’s walk through the main exception types Odoo provides that are out of the box.

1. UserError - Friendly Feedback for Invalid Actions

				
					odoo.exceptions.UserError(message)

The UserError exception is designed for scenarios where the user attempts an invalid action based on a record's current state. It is akin to HTTP 400-level errors, meaning the fault lies with the client.

Use Case: Trying to confirm a sales order that lacks a customer.

Why Use It:  

  • It informs the user of what went wrong.
  • It prevents operations that would cause system inconsistency.
  • It mirrors a 400-level HTTP error: a client-side issue the user can correct.

2. Redirect Warning – Errors with a Built-in Fix 

				
					odoo.exceptions.RedirectWarning(message, action_id, button_text, additional_context=None)

Unlike most exceptions, RedirectWarning does more than just throw an error—it guides the user toward a corrective action.

  • message: What will the user see in the model?
  • action_id: ID of the action to redirect to.
  • button_text: Label for the redirect button.
  • additional_context: Optional context dictionary for the redirection.

Use Case: A customer record is incomplete, and the user must be redirected to complete it.

Why Use It:  

  • It reduces user frustration.
  • It updates workflows by guiding users directly to the fix.
  • It enhances user experience with actionable messages.

3. Access Denied – Handling Login Failures Gracefully

odoo.exceptions.AccessDenied(message='Access Denied')

 

This exception is thrown during login attempts with invalid credentials. It is special because it doesn't show a traceback, making it cleaner and more secure.

Thrown during login attempts with incorrect credentials.

Key Point: This exception does not generate a traceback.

Use Case: Failed login due to incorrect username/password.

Why Use It:  

  • Prevents stack traces from being shown during authentication failures.
    Keeps sensitive operations secure and clean.
    Offers a straightforward message without overwhelming the user.

4. Access Error – Enforcing Security at the Data Level

				
					odoo.exceptions.AccessError(message)

Raised when the user tries to access data for which they don’t have permissions.

Use Case: Reading a confidential employee record without appropriate rights.

Why Use It:

  • Enforces role-based access control.
  • Protects sensitive information.
  • Provides a clear message instead of crashing or failing silently.

5. Cache Miss – A Developer's Debugging Ally 

				
					odoo.exceptions.CacheMiss(record, field)

Indicates that a requested field value is missing from the ORM cache.

Use Case: Reading a field after the cache has been cleared or flushed.

Why Use It:  

  • Helps developers identify issues with cache usage.
  • Useful during module development or performance tuning.
  • It should never reach the UI in a production environment.

6. Missing Error – Catching Disappearing Records

				
					odoo.exceptions.MissingError(message)

Triggered when trying to operate on a record that no longer exists in the database.

Use Case: Attempting to update or delete a record that was already removed.

Why Use It:  

  • Prevents operations on stale or invalid data.
  • Helps maintain database consistency.
  • Provides clear feedback when records disappear unexpectedly.

7. Validation Error – Enforcing Business Logic

				
					odoo.exceptions.ValidationError(message)

This is raised when a Python constraint (such as a unique field) is violated.

Use Case: Creating a user with a login already in the system.

Why Use It:  

  • Prevents duplicate or invalid data from entering the system.
  • Ensures business rules are strictly enforced.
  • Improves overall application stability and data quality.

Best Practices for Handling Error Management in Odoo

Now that we've covered the core exceptions, here are some practical tips to help you use them effectively:

  • Always raise meaningful errors: Avoid generic or vague messages. Be clear and direct.
  • Use UserError generously for anything that the user can correct.
  • Utilise RedirectWarning to improve flow, especially in complex user journeys.
  • Never expose technical errors to end users; they’re for developers, not customers.
  • Log exceptions where appropriate to aid debugging and support.
  • Test exception scenarios as part of your module’s QA process.

A Well-Structured System for Error Management in Odoo

It provides a thoughtful and well-structured system for error management in Odoo through its built-in exception classes. Using them properly allows developers to:

  • Protect users from system errors
  • Communicate problems clearly
  • Guide users toward resolving issues
  • Maintain high standards of security and data integrity.

Choosing the right exception at the right time ensures that your applications are not only end-user friendly but also maintainable.

Whether building a new module from scratch or extending an existing one, exception handling should never be an afterthought. It’s a powerful tool for improving the quality of your code and your users' satisfaction.

Title: How to Create and Configure Server Actions in Odoo 17?
Content:
Server Actions in Odoo serve as a dynamic mechanism for automating processes without the need for extensive custom development. These actions enable users to define a sequence of operations or tasks that the system executes automatically under specific conditions. From creating records and updating fields to triggering complex business logic, Server Actions empower users to automate routine activities and respond intelligently to various scenarios within the ERP environment.

In this blog, we will explore the steps to create and configure Server Actions in Odoo 17, using a practical example to demonstrate their application.

Understanding Server Actions in Odoo 17

Server Actions enable automation without requiring extensive custom development. A server action can perform the following types of actions.

  1. Execute a python code
  2. Create new record
  3. Update new record
  4. Sent an email
  5. Sent SMS message
  6. Add followers
  7. Create next activity
  8. Execute multiple actions

To view all the server actions available in the Odoo system, enable debug mode, then go to Settings -> Technical -> Server Actions.

This is the list of existing server actions in Odoo 17.

Steps to Create and Configure Server Actions in Odoo

Let’s create a Server Action that copies data from the phone field to the mobile field in the ‘res.partners’ model. This action will update records dynamically when executed.

Step 1: Define the Server Action in XML

The server action should be defined in the “ir_action_data.xml” file inside the “data” directory of your module. Add the following code:

				
					
   Copy phone to mobile
   list
   code
   action = records.action_copy_phone_to_mobile()

Here’s what each field in the XML represents:

  • name: specifies the name of the server action, which shows on the server actions menu.
  • model_id: is the model linked to the server action, it should be in this form <module>.model_<model_name>
  • binding_model_id:  It specifies that the action is bound to the referencing model.
  • binding_view_types: specifies the action is intended to be available in which views of the associated model.
  • state: It specifies the type of server action we discussed above, in our case, we choose it as “code” for executing a Python script.
  • code: specify the Python script to be executed.

Step 2: Define the Python Function

After adding the XML code, next, include the Python function referenced in the XML within the res.partner model. You should include the function “action_copy_phone_to_mobile()” in the res.partner model, as mentioned in the server action.

				
					def action_copy_phone_to_mobile(self):
   for record in self:
       if record.phone and not record.mobile:
           record.write({'mobile': record.phone})

This function checks if the phone field is filled and the mobile field is empty. If both conditions are met, it copies the value from the phone field to the mobile field.

Step 3: Use the Server Action

Now, we can use this server action on the contacts list view.

Select some contacts that do not have mobile fields and have phone fields, then under the “Actions” menu, there will be a newly created server action “Copy phone to mobile” button.

Step 4: Verify the Results

When the Server Action is executed, the selected records will be updated. The values from the phone field will be copied to the mobile field. You can verify this by checking the updated records in the list view. The result would be.

Accessing Server Actions

The newly created server action is also visible in Server actions in the Technical menu from settings.

Simplifying Automation with Server Actions

In summary, Odoo Server Actions empower users to automate diverse processes, enhancing efficiency and reducing manual intervention, thereby optimizing operations within the ERP environment.

By following the steps outlined in this blog, you can create a custom Server Action to address your specific business needs. Whether it’s automating updates, triggering workflows, or sending notifications, Server Actions simplify the process and optimize operations within the ERP system.

Invoicing Policies for Timesheets in Odoo 18

Odoo 18 provides businesses with flexibility in billing for timesheets by offering two distinct invoicing policies. Depending on the company’s workflow and service model, users can choose:

  1. All Recorded Timesheets – Every hour logged is billable, even if not approved.
  2. Validated Timesheets Only – Only manager-approved timesheets are billed.

Let’s go through both policies step by step.

All Recorded Timesheets

Enable the Policy

  • Click Create Invoice → Draft Invoice → Confirm to finalize.

Validated Timesheets Only

With this option, timesheets must be approved by a manager before invoicing. This is useful when some hours (e.g., internal support work) should not be charged to clients.

Manager Validation

  • Go to Timesheets > To Validate.
  • Review employee timesheets for the last period (week, month, or custom).
  • Select the timesheets to be approved and use Action > Validate.

Invoice Only Approved Hours

  • Once validated, the approved hours are locked from editing.
  • Go to the linked sales order → the delivered Time reflects only approved hours.
  • Click Create Invoice, confirm the draft, and post the invoice.

Title: How to Create Powerful Dashboards in Odoo 18
Content:
Dashboards In Odoo 18 deliver an organized visual presentation of essential business data. Users can  track essential metrics through dashboards to monitor performance and make efficient decisions. Odoo 18 provides users  with improved dashboard creation capabilities because of its enhanced tools and better user interface. The powerful flexible ERP system  Odoo enables multiple methods to present and handle data. The views system in Odoo 18 determines  how users interact with records throughout different modules. The views system improves user experience through organized layouts that present  information in an attractive manner.

This blog provides a complete guide to building custom dashboards in Odoo  18 starting from fundamental setup through advanced customization. This guide serves both developers and business users to create  customized dashboards that fulfill their particular requirements. Let’s get started!

In Odoo 18  client actions function as the mechanism to display dashboards. Users can access interactive and dynamic dashboard views through  menu items which trigger these actions.

Defining the Client Action

To render a custom dashboard, we need to define a client action in the ir.actions.client model. This action links the dashboard to a specific JavaScript component via a tag.

				
					<record id="crm_dashboard_action" model="ir.actions.client">
  <field name="name">CRM Dashboard</field>
  <field name="tag">crm_dashboard_tag</field>
</record>
<menuitem name="Dashboard" id="crm_dashboard"      
         sequence="0" action="crm_dashboard_action"
         parent="crm.crm_menu_root"/>

* ‘name’ field: Defines the display name of the dashboard in Odoo.

* ‘tag’ field: Links the JavaScript file with the client action.

When the "Dashboard" menu item is clicked, it triggers crm_dashboard_action, which then connects to the JavaScript file via the specified tag (crm_dashboard_tag).

Creating the JavaScript Component

Next, we create a JavaScript component that will handle the rendering of the dashboard. Create a JavaScript file in static/src/js/dashboard.js:

				
					/** @odoo-module **/
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { Component } from "@odoo/owl";
const actionRegistry = registry.category("actions");
class CrmDashboard extends Component {}
CrmDashboard.template = "my_module.CrmDashboard";
// Register the component with the action tag
actionRegistry.add("crm_dashboard_tag", CrmDashboard);

* The JavaScript file imports Odoo's Owl framework to define a dashboard component.

* The actionRegistry.add() method connects the component to the crm_dashboard_tag, ensuring it is triggered when the action is called.

* The component uses an XML template to define the dashboard’s UI.

At this stage, the user interface will display a blank dashboard view.

Creating the Dashboard Template

To display content inside the dashboard, we need to create an XML template. Create an XML file in static/src/xml/dashboard.xml:

				
					<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<templates>
   <t t-name="my_module.CrmDashboard">
               <center>
                   <h1 style="margin:20px;">CRM Dashboard</h1>
               </center>
   </t>
</templates>

* The template defines a simple heading ("CRM Dashboard") centered on the page.

* This template is linked to the JavaScript component through the t-name="my_module.CrmDashboard" attribute.

Adding Files to the Manifest

To ensure the JavaScript and XML files are loaded correctly, they must be included in the module’s __manifest__.py file:

				
					'assets': {
   'web.assets_backend': [
       'my_module/static/src/js/dashboard.js',
       'my_module/static/src/xml/dashboard.xml',
   ],
},

This ensures that the dashboard assets are properly loaded in the Odoo backend.

After completing these steps, you will have a functional blank dashboard integrated into Odoo 18. You can now expand it by adding widgets, charts, and other interactive components to enhance usability.

Adding Tiles to the Odoo Dashboard

Now let's add tiles to the Odoo dashboard and fetch data dynamically using ORM calls in JavaScript.

HTML Structure for Tiles:

				
					
   <!-- Lead Tile-->
                           <i

class CrmLead(models.Model):

Title: How Do Mixins in Odoo 18 Improve Code Reusability & Project Efficiency?
Content:
The development of Odoo requires developers to build modular code that remains maintainable and reusable for various business needs. The use of classical inheritance and composition enables model extension and feature addition but creates rigid or tangled hierarchies particularly in large complex projects. Odoo developers use Mixins as a Python programming pattern to add shared functionality across multiple models beyond traditional deep inheritance limitations.

Mixins have become more important in Odoo 18 than in previous versions. Through Mixins developers can wrap up repeated logic such as change tracking and attachment management and notification handling to make them accessible for any model that requires these features. The approach helps maintain a DRY codebase while providing better maintenance and evolution capabilities for applications when business requirements shift.

This article explains Mixins in detail including their definition and Odoo 18 implementation and their essential role for developers who want to create powerful Odoo modules. The knowledge of Mixins enables you to achieve better project efficiency and adaptability in your Odoo work while streamlining your code and speeding up feature delivery for your team

What is a Mixin?

The mixin in Odoo functions as a particular model type which enables the sharing of reusable behaviors and logic between multiple models through code reuse instead of complex inheritance structures. Mixins exist as abstract models (models.AbstractModel) which do not automatically generate database tables unless developers explicitly define them.

The inheritance of a mixin in your primary model enables you to directly add features such as messaging and activity tracking and archiving and logging capabilities to that model. The approach enables code reusability and modularity and consistency which results in a cleaner and more efficient codebase. The built-in mail.thread mixin in Odoo provides messaging and activity features but developers can create custom mixins to add any shared functionality they require

Common Built-in Mixins in Odoo 18

Odoo provides several powerful built-in mixins. Here are a few commonly used ones:

1. mail.thread

Enables messaging and communication logging on your model (chatter functionality).

class MyModel(models.Model):

    _name = 'my.model'

    _inherit = ['mail.thread']

✔️ Adds chatter to your form views.
✔️ Automatically tracks changes in fields marked with tracking=True.

2. mail.activity.mixin

Adds support for scheduled activities (e.g., To Do, Call, Email).

class MyModel(models.Model):

    _name = 'my.model'

    _inherit = ['mail.activity.mixin']

✔️ Enables the “Schedule Activity” widget.
✔️ Integrates with the mail.activity model.

How Mixins Work in Odoo Internals

  • Odoo mixins are standard Python classes that inherit from models.AbstractModel.
  • They are often registered with _name starting with a dot (.) or without _name at all, indicating they are not standalone models.
  • When inherited, their methods, computed fields, and constraints get merged into the child class.

Creating a Custom Mixin

Suppose we want a mixin that auto-generates a unique reference code for any model that inherits it.

				
					from odoo import models, fields, api
class UniqueCodeMixin(models.AbstractModel):
    _name = 'mymodule.unique.code.mixin'
    _description = 'Unique Code Mixin'
    unique_code = fields.Char(string='Unique Code', readonly=True)
    @api.model
    def create(self, vals):
        vals['unique_code'] = self.env['ir.sequence'].next_by_code('mymodule.unique.code') or '/'
        return super().create(vals)
Now you can inherit it in your actual model:
class MyCustomer(models.Model):
    _name = 'mymodule.customer'
    _inherit = ['mymodule.unique.code.mixin']

Benefits of Using Mixins in Odoo 18

Code Reusability

Mixins enable developers to create reusable code blocks which they can apply to multiple models without repeating themselves. The practice of code reuse through mixins reduces development time while automatically updating shared logic across all mixin implementations.

Standardized Behaviors

The practice of placing common features into mixins enables uniform application of behaviors such as logging and notifications and access control across all relevant models. The standardization process enhances both the reliability and predictability of your application.

Cleaner and Modular Codebase

Mixins enable developers to create modular code by separating reusable logic from core business models. The organized structure of your codebase becomes easier to read and maintain as your application expands because of mixins.

Ease of Maintenance

The maintenance process for shared functionality becomes simple when using mixins because modifications need to be made only once. The changes you make to a mixin will automatically affect all models that use this mixin. The maintenance process becomes less complex while the risk of errors and inconsistencies decreases

When Not to Use Mixins

While mixins are powerful, overusing or misusing them can cause:

  • Inheritance conflicts if multiple mixins override the same method.
  • Reduced clarity, especially for new developers trying to trace field or method origins.
  • Unnecessary overhead if features are not usedUse mixins when you need shared functionality across many models, not for one-off behaviors.

Pro Tips

  • Use models.AbstractModel for all mixins to avoid unintended database tables.
  • Document clearly what your custom mixin does.
  • Prefer _inherit = [] syntax over super() method chaining when possible, to keep method calls predictable.

Mixins for Scalable and Maintainable Solutions

Mixins in Odoo 18 enable developers to create model logic enhancements through modular and reusable code blocks. The abstract model definition of mixins enables you to include shared features like messaging and activity tracking and logging and business logic which models can inherit without code duplication or deep inheritance structures.

The Odoo platform includes built-in mixins which include mail.thread for messaging and activity tracking as well as portal.mixin for portal access functionality so developers can easily implement complex model features with minimal development effort. You can develop personalized mixins to fulfill your business needs by implementing automatic change logging and reusable fields and methods across various models.

The approach maintains a clean codebase through modularity and simplicity while ensuring easy maintenance because all inheriting models automatically receive mixin updates. The combination of built-in and custom mixins enables you to develop flexible and scalable and maintainable Odoo applications which efficiently support business needs evolution

Title: How to Automate Employee Birthday Reminders in Odoo 18 Using Scheduled Emails?
Content:
Sending Birthday Reminders in Odoo 18 Using Automated Emails

Employee birthdays are an essential part of workplace culture. They offer a chance to celebrate and appreciate your staff. However, keeping track of every employee’s birthday manually can be a daunting task for HR teams. This is where automation can make a huge difference. By automating birthday reminders, you ensure that no employee is overlooked, and HR managers can plan for celebrations or greetings. This blog post’ll show you how to set up an automated birthday reminders in Odoo 18. This system will help HR teams to:

  • Identify employees who have birthdays coming up in the next 3 days
  • Notify HR managers via email
  • Run automatically every day using a scheduled cron job (ir.cron)

Let’s get into the steps!

Why Automate Birthday Reminders?

In many organizations, birthdays are more than just a personal milestone. They serve as an opportunity to show appreciation and boost employee morale. A thoughtful birthday greeting can go a long way in strengthening the relationship between employees and their managers. However, manually tracking and sending these automate reminders can be time-consuming and prone to errors.

By automating this process, HR teams will have one less task to worry about, and they can focus on what truly matters: making their employees feel valued. Automation also ensures that no birthday is missed, even during busy times.

Step 1: Add the Python Method to Handle Birthday Notifications

The first step is to extend the hr.employee model and create the logic for sending the birthday reminders. We will create a method called _notify_hr_employee_birthday() that will identify employees with birthdays coming up in the next 3 days and send email reminders to the assigned HR managers.

In this step, we will use Odoo’s ORM to query the hr.employee model for employees whose birthdays match the target date (3 days from the current date). We will also filter out employees who do not have an assigned HR manager.

Here’s the Python code to achieve this:

				
					from datetime import timedelta
from odoo import api, fields, models
class HrEmployee(models.Model):
   _inherit = 'hr.employee'
   hr_managers_ids = fields.Many2many(
       'res.users',
       string='HR Managers',
       help='HR users to notify about this employee’s birthday'
   )
   @api.model
   def _notify_hr_employee_birthday(self):
       today = fields.Date.today()
       target_day = today + timedelta(days=3)
       employees = self.search([('birthday', '=', target_day)])
       if not employees:
           return
       template = self.env.ref('employee_birthday_reminder.email_template_birthday_reminder')
       for employee in employees:
           for hr_user in employee.hr_managers_ids.filtered(lambda u: u.email):
               if template:
                   template.send_mail(employee.id, force_send=True, email_values={
                       'email_to': hr_user.email,
                   })

Step 2: Email Template XML

Next, we need to create an email template to notify HR managers about upcoming birthdays. This template will include placeholders for the employee’s name and birthday, which will be dynamically replaced when the email is sent.

Here's the XML code to create the email template:

				
					<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<odoo>
   <data>
       <record id="email_template_birthday_reminder" model="mail.template">
           <field name="name">Employee Birthday Reminder</field>
           <field name="model_id" ref="hr.model_hr_employee"/>
           <field name="subject">Upcoming Birthday: {{ object.name }}</field>
           <field name="email_from">${(object.company_id.email or 'info@example.com')|safe}</field>
           <field name="body_html" type="html">
                   <p>Dear HR Manager,
                   </p>
                   <p>This is a reminder that
                       <strong>
                           <t t-out="object.name"/>
                       </strong>
                       has a birthday coming up on
                       <strong>
                           <t t-out="object.birthday"/>
                       </strong>
                       .
                   </p>
                   <p>Please plan accordingly!</p>
                   <p>Best Regards,<br/>Thank you.
                   </p>
           </field>
       </record>
   </data>
</odoo>

In this template:

  • The subject field dynamically includes the employee’s name.
  • The body_html contains the employee’s name and birthday date, which will be filled in at runtime.

This simple, yet effective email template will ensure HR managers are always notified in advance of employee birthdays.

Step 3: Add the Scheduled Action (Cron Job)

The final step is to set up a scheduled cron job to run the birthday reminders in Odoo 18 process automatically daily. This will ensure that the reminder system works without requiring any manual intervention.

We’ll use Odoo’s ir.cron model to create a scheduled action that triggers the _notify_hr_employee_birthday() method daily.

Here’s the XML code to set up the cron job:

				
					<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<odoo>
   <data>
       <record id="ir_cron_notify_birthday" model="ir.cron">
           <field name="name">Employee Birthday Reminder</field>
           <field name="model_id" ref="hr.model_hr_employee"/>
           <field name="state">code</field>
           <field name="code">model._notify_hr_employee_birthday()</field>
           <field name="interval_number">1</field>
           <field name="interval_type">days</field>
           <field name="active" eval="True"/>
           <field name="nextcall"
                  eval="(DateTime.now().replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')"/>
       </record>
   </data>
</odoo>

This cron job will execute every day at midnight, checking for upcoming birthdays and sending reminders as needed. It will keep running automatically without any intervention from HR staff.

Final Output

Once the system is set up, HR managers will receive an email 3 days before any employee’s birthday. This automation eliminates the need for HR teams to track birthdays, ensuring no special day is forgotten manually.

Benefits of Automating Birthday Reminders

  1. Time-Saving: Automating the process eliminates the need for HR staff to check each employee’s birthday manually.
  2. No Birthdays Missed: The cron job runs every day, so HR managers are always notified ahead of time.
  3. Improved Employee Morale: Timely birthday greetings can help create a positive work environment, leading to happier and more engaged employees.
  4. Increased Efficiency: HR teams can focus on more important tasks rather than spending time on routine reminders.

Birthday Reminders in Odoo 18

Following these steps, you’ve successfully set up automated birthday reminders in Odoo 18! With the system running daily via the scheduled cron job, HR managers will always have a heads-up about upcoming birthdays, allowing them to plan celebrations and greetings easily.

This small automation can make a massive difference in improving workplace morale and ensuring your employees feel appreciated. So, why not add this little extra appreciation to your workplace?

Title: How to Override Methods or Models in Odoo 18
Content:
Odoo, one of the most popular open-source ERP systems, provides immense flexibility and customization options to adapt the software to your unique companies needs. Whether you want to add custom fields, modify business logic, or change the system's behaviour, Odoo allows you to extend and override its built-in models and methods without altering its core code.

The ability to override methods or models in Odoo is a critical feature that allows businesses to tailor Odoo’s functionality to specific processes. With the flexibility of Odoo's powerful object-relational mapping (ORM) framework, developers can safely customize the system to ensure upgrade compatibility and maintain clean code practices.

In this blog, we’ll explore:

  1. How to Override a Model
  2. How to Override a Method (Standard and Computed)
  3. Best Practices for Customization (Odoo Customization services)

How to Override a Model

Override methods or models in Odoo represent the data structure for various business objects like customers, products, sales orders, etc. Overriding a model allows you to add new fields, modify existing fields, or extend the functionality of Odoo’s built-in models.

Steps to Override a Model:

Inherit the Model in Python:

To override methods or models in Odoo, the first step is to inherit the existing model in your custom module. You can do this by creating a new Python class that extends the desired model. For example, if you want to add a custom field to the res.partner model (which represents partners or customers), the Python code would look like this:

				
					from odoo import models, fields
class ResPartner(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'res.partner'  # Inheriting existing model
    x_custom_field = fields.Char(string="Custom Field")

In this example, we add a new x_custom_field of type Char (a text field) to the res.partner model. Using the inherit attribute, we extend the model and add the new field, appearing in all partner-related forms and views.

Update the View in XML:

After modifying the override methods or models in Odoo, you need to update the corresponding form view in XML like Odoo XML RPC to display the new field. Odoo’s views define how the model data is presented to the user in the interface. To update the form view for the res.partner model, use the following XML code:

				
					<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_partner_form_inherit_custom" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">res.partner.inherit.form</field>
        <field name="model">res.partner</field>
        <field name="inherit_id" ref="base.view_partner_form"/>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">
                   <field name="name" position="after">
                <field name="x_custom_field"/>
            </field>
        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

In this XML code:

  • We reference the original partner form view (base.view_partner_form).
  • Using the inherit_id attribute, we tell Odoo that we’re modifying this existing view.
  • The position="after" attribute places the new x_custom_field right after the name field in the form.

This ensures that the new field will appear smoothly in the user interface without breaking the original layout.

How to Override a Method in Odoo

Override methods or models in Odoo define the behavior of models. You can override built-in methods to customize how records are created, updated, or deleted and modify business logic in computations or actions triggered by buttons.

Overriding the Create Method:

The create method is one of the most commonly overridden methods in Odoo. This method is called when a new record is created in the database. For instance, if you want to automatically capitalize the name field when creating a new partner, You can override:

  • Regular methods (e.g., create, write, unlink)
  • Compute methods
  • Button or action methods

Overriding the create method:

The create method is one of the most commonly overridden methods in Odoo. This method is called when a new record is created in the database. For instance, if you want to automatically capitalize the name field when creating a new partner, you can override the create method like this:

This is the code will write in python file

				
					from odoo import models, fields, api
class ResPartner(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'res.partner'
    @api.model_create_multi
    def create(self, vals_list):
        for vals in vals_list:
            if 'name' in vals and vals['name']:
                vals['name'] = vals['name'].upper()
        return super().create(vals_list)

Overriding a Compute Method:

Computed fields in Odoo are fields whose value is calculated dynamically based on other fields. You can override the compute method for a field to modify how the value is calculated.

For example, let’s say we have a sale.order model with a custom computed field called custom_total, which calculates the total value of all order lines. Here’s how you can override the compute method:

				
					from odoo import models, fields, api
class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'
    custom_total = fields.Float(string="Custom Total", compute="_compute_custom_total")
    @api.depends('order_line')
    def _compute_custom_total(self):
        for record in self:
            record.custom_total = sum(line.price_total for line in record.order_line)

Best Practices for Overriding Models and Method

When overriding methods or models in Odoo, it’s important to follow best practices to ensure the stability and maintainability of your Odoo instance. Here are some key practices to keep in mind:

1. Always Use super() When Overriding Core Methods

Using super() ensures that the original functionality of the method is preserved. If you override a method like create or write, always call the parent method to maintain the existing behavior unless you want to completely replace it.

For example:

				
					return super().create(vals_list)

This ensures that the create method works as expected, even after adding custom logic.

2. Use ORM Methods for Database Operations

Avoid using raw SQL queries to interact with the database. Instead, use Odoo’s ORM methods (create, write, unlink, etc.) to handle database operations. These methods ensure that the data is properly validated, and they trigger the necessary automated actions (such as updating related records).

For example, always use

				
					record.write({'field_name': value})

Instead of directly updating the database.

3. Add Module Dependencies

If your module depends on other modules (for example, if you inherit models from them), be sure to add those dependencies in the __manifest__.py file. This ensures that Odoo loads the required modules before yours.

Example of adding a dependency:

				
					{
    'name': 'Custom Module',
    'depends': ['base', 'sale'],
    'data': ['views.xml'],
}

This tells Odoo that your custom module depends on the base and sale modules.

4. Thorough Testing Is Crucial

Customization is powerful but should be done carefully. Overriding core methods such as create, write, or unlink can have significant effects on your data and application behavior. Always test your customizations thoroughly in a development environment before deploying them to production.

Create test cases for each method you override and validate that your custom logic works as expected.

For clear code we can follow these steps:

Always use super() when overriding core methods to maintain original functionality unless you fully replace it.

Avoid direct database changes. Use ORM methods (create, write, unlink).

Add module dependencies in __manifest__.py if you inherit models from them.

Test thoroughly, especially if overriding sensitive methods like create, write, or unlink.

Override Methods or Models in Odoo

Odoo’s flexibility allows you to easily adapt the system to your business needs by overriding models and methods. Whether adding custom fields, modifying existing behaviour, or introducing new business logic, understanding how to override models and methods correctly is essential for ensuring that your customizations are effective and maintainable.

By following the best practices discussed in this blog, such as using super(), relying on Odoo’s ORM methods, and thoroughly testing your changes, you can create robust and customized solutions for your business while ensuring compatibility with future Odoo updates.

Odoo’s ORM framework provides a clean, safe, and scalable way to implement customizations without altering the core code. As your business grows, your Odoo instance can grow with it, adapting seamlessly to changing needs.

Title: How to Create & Manage the Deferred Expense in Odoo 18 Accounting Module?
Content:
Understanding the Odoo 18 Deferred Expenses

Managing finances efficiently is paramount for any business, and when handling expenses that span multiple accounting periods, manage the deferred expense becomes essential. In Odoo 18 Accounting, companies can simplify the process of managing costs deferred, ensuring accuracy and compliance with accounting standards.

Deferred or prepaid expenses are costs that a business pays in advance for goods or services to be received in the future. Properly managing these expenses in Odoo 18 ensures that financial statements accurately reflect the company's financial health.

In this guide, we'll dive deep into how to create and manage the deferred expense in the Odoo 18 Accounting Module. We'll cover everything from setting up deferred expenses to configuring accounts, recording journal entries, and generating insightful reports. Whether you're a business owner, accountant, or Odoo user, this comprehensive tutorial will help you master the art of managing deferred expenses in Odoo 18. Let’s get started on this accounting journey with Odoo 18!

What are Deferred Expenses?

Deferred expenses are costs that a business incurs upfront but are recognized as expenses over time as the benefits of those costs are realized. This accounting practice helps match expenses with the revenue they generate, providing a clearer picture of financial performance.

For example, a company paying $14,000 for a one-year insurance policy wouldn’t immediately record the entire amount as an expense. Instead, it would allocate $2,000 as an expense each month, deferring the rest until future periods.

Key Characteristics of Deferred Expenses

  • Paid in advance for future benefits
  • Recognized gradually over time
  • Common in rent, insurance, subscriptions, etc.

Understanding how to handle these expenses correctly in Odoo 18 ensures compliance with accounting principles like the matching concept and accrual basis accounting.

Why Use Deferred Expenses in Odoo 18 Accounting?

Managing deferred expenses effectively in Odoo 18 Accounting offers several benefits:

Accurate Financial Reporting: Ensures expenses are matched with corresponding revenue.

Improved Cash Flow Management: Helps track prepaid costs and forecast future financial obligations.

Regulatory Compliance: Aligns with accounting standards and regulations.

Automation Efficiency: Odoo 18 simplifies the process with automated calculations and schedules.

By leveraging Odoo 18's robust accounting features, businesses can automate deferred expense recognition, reduce manual errors and save time.

The Importance of Configuration in Odoo 18 Deferred Expenses

Setting up deferred expenses correctly is the foundation of effective expense management. The Odoo 18 deferred expense configuration process is intuitive, allowing users to define rules that govern how expenses are deferred. This configuration ensures that the deferral process aligns with the company’s accounting policies.

The proper configuration also impacts the accuracy of Odoo 18 deferred expense journal entries. When the system is set up correctly, journal entries are generated automatically, reflecting the correct accounting periods. This decreases the risk of errors and ensures compliance with accounting standards.

Practical Benefits of Using Odoo 18 for Deferred Expenses

The practical benefits of managing deferred expenses in Odoo 18 Accounting are numerous. First, automation reduces the administrative burden, freeing resources for more strategic tasks. Second, the accuracy of Odoo 18 deferred expense journal entries ensures that financial statements are reliable. Journal entries are automatically created to move amounts from the deferred expense account to the expense account as per the schedule.

Additionally, Odoo 18's flexible deferred expense configuration allows businesses to modify the system to their specific needs. This Odoo customization ensures that deferred expenses are managed in a way that aligns with business objectives and regulatory requirements.

Insights from Odoo 18 Deferred Expense Reporting

Reporting is critical to managing deferred expenses. Odoo 18 deferred expense reporting allows businesses to analyze expense data comprehensively. These reports can be customized to show specific periods, expense categories, or other relevant metrics.

With Odoo 18 Accounting, businesses can generate real-time reports, offering immediate insights into deferred expenses. This capability is vital for financial forecasting and budgeting, as it provides a clear picture of future costs and their impact on economic performance.

How Does Odoo 18 Manage the Deferred Expense in Accounting

While recording deferred expenses is crucial, managing them effectively over time is equally important. Odoo 18 provides robust tools to help businesses manage costs deferred flawlessly.

To manage deferred expenses in Odoo 18, go directly to the Accounting Module in your Odoo dashboard.

Go to Configuration > Settings.

Simply scroll down. Under the Default Accounts section, the amount computed is based on three categories: days, months, and all months. So, I can set it based on ‘‘Days’’ and then click Save.

After that, go to the Vendors menu and click on Bill.

Click on ‘‘New’’.

Title: How to Hide Specific Modules in Odoo 18 for Certain Users
Content:
In Odoo, businesses must often customize their ERP system to fit operational needs. One common requirement is restricting access to specific modules or features for different groups of users. This can be crucial for ensuring that only authorized users can access sensitive or specialized data, such as financial records or, in this case, the Rental module. In this blog, we’ll explore how you can hide specific modules in Odoo 18, using the Rental module as an example.

Why Hide Specific Modules in Odoo 18?

As organizations grow, their requirements for managing user roles and access control become more complex. Let’s say you run a business that offers multiple services, but you want to limit the visibility of certain apps for specific users. For instance, you may want to give employees in your sales or support departments access to general functionalities but restrict access to modules related to rental equipment, which is only relevant to your operations team.

Hide specific modules in Odoo 18 is not just about hiding menu items but can be done more robustly. By restricting the entire module, you can ensure that users never even see the option to interact with sensitive features. This blog will show you exactly how to accomplish this by hiding the Rental module from users in a custom user group called "Non Rental".

Use Case

Imagine you have a group of employees who work in various departments but are not involved in Rental operations. You don’t want these employees to see the Rental module in their Odoo dashboard. By following the steps outlined below, you can create a custom group (group_non_rental) and use Odoo’s menu system to dynamically hide this module from the users in that group.

  1. Creating a custom group (group_non_rental)
  2. Inheriting ir.ui.menu to control visibility of the menu dynamically
  3. Using the discard() method to remove the Rental menu from their view

Step 1: Define the Group

The first step is to define a new security group in Odoo. This group will represent users who should not have access to the Rental module.

The security group controls which menus, views, and modules users can access. In our case, we’ll create a group called "Non Rental" that prevents users from seeing the Rental module.

Let’s start by defining the group in the security/groups.xml file

				
					<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<odoo>
   <data>
       <record id="group_non_rental" model="res.groups">
           <field name="name">Non Rental</field>
       </record>
   </data>
</odoo>

Here’s what’s happening:

  • group_non_rental: This defines a new security group named "Non Rental".
  • Once this group is created, you can assign users to it, which will restrict their access to the Rental module.

Step 2: Override Menu Visibility Logic

The next step is to control the visibility of menus based on the user's group. Odoo’s menu system is flexible; we can override it to hide specific menus conditionally. For this, we will extend the ir.ui.menu model to customise which menus are visible to which users. 

Use the _visible_menu_ids Method to control which menus are visible to users. By overriding this method, we can programmatically exclude specific menus for users in the "Non Rental" group.

 

models/ir_ui_menu.py

from odoo import models, api

				
					class IrUiMenu(models.Model):
   _inherit = 'ir.ui.menu'
   @api.model
   def _visible_menu_ids(self, debug=False):
       menus = super()._visible_menu_ids(debug)
       if self.env.user.has_group('sdm_rental_equipment.group_non_rental'):
           menus.discard(self.env.ref('sale_renting.rental_menu_root').id)
       return menus

 Explanation of the Code:

  • super()._visible_menu_ids() gets the default list of visible menus.
  • self.env.user.has_group(...) checks if the current user is in the "Non Rental" group.
  • menus.discard(...) removes the Rental menu from the visible list if the condition is met.

This method works with Odoo’s native menu system, so there’s no need for complex workarounds or hacks. You modify the visibility logic and use the built-in discard() method to remove unwanted menus.

Step 3: Assign the Group to Specific Users

Now that we’ve defined the group and the logic to hide the Rental module, the next step is to assign the "Non Rental" group to specific users through the Odoo User Management interface.

  1. Go to Settings → Users & Companies → Users.
  2. Open the form view for the user you want to restrict.
  3. Under the Other Groups section, check the box for the Non-Rental group.

By assigning users to this group, they will no longer see the Rental module in their dashboard.

Result

Once you’ve completed these steps, users in the "Non Rental" group will no longer see the Rental module in their Odoo interface. This hides the menu items and ensures the entire Rental app is inaccessible to them.

Bonus Tip: Extend This to More Menus

What if you need to hide more than just the Rental module? The process is incredibly flexible, and you can extend the logic to hide additional modules for specific user groups.

You can easily extend the logic to hide other modules:

				
					if self.env.user.has_group('your_module.group_no_accounting'):
   menus.discard(self.env.ref('account.menu_finance').id)

This will ensure that the Accounting menu is hidden for users in the "group_no_accounting" group.

How It Works for Other Modules:

This method can be extended to any module or menu in Odoo. Simply identify the menu item you want to hide and use the discard() method with the appropriate menu reference. For example:

  • Sales Module: menus.discard(self.env.ref('sale.menu_sale_order').id)
  • Inventory Module: menus.discard(self.env.ref('stock.menu_stock_inventory').id)

Why This Method Works

This approach leverages Odoo’s native menu system, ensuring a clean and efficient way of managing menu visibility. Unlike other methods (like using record rules), this method doesn't require complex configurations and is entirely based on modifying the menu rendering logic. It’s also scalable and can be applied to multiple user groups and menus across the system.

Here’s why this approach is practical:

  • No reliance on record rules: Unlike access control lists (ACLs) or record rules, this method works purely on the UI and menu structure, making it less prone to issues when data or access changes.
  • Cleaner user interface: By dynamically hiding entire menus, users are not distracted by irrelevant options, making their workflow more intuitive and efficient.
  • Flexible and extensible: You can easily add additional menu restrictions as your business grows, without complicated changes to the underlying structure.

Hide Specific Modules in Odoo 18

With just a few lines of code, you can elegantly hide entire modules from specific users. This method:

  • Doesn’t rely on record rules
  • Works with Odoo's native menu visibility system
  • Keeps the UI clean for users with limited access

With this solution, you’ll improve your system’s efficiency and reduce users' complexity, giving them a more focused and tailored experience.

By Hide specific modules in Odoo 18 and controlling access, you ensure that your team can focus on what matters most, without the distractions of unnecessary functionalities.

Title: How to Manage Deferred Revenue in Odoo 18 Accounting?
Content:
Understanding the Odoo 18 Deferred Revenue Management

Have you ever worked to recognize revenue at the right time in your business? Or perhaps you’ve received payments in advance for a service or product you’ll deliver over time, but you're unsure how to manage and report that revenue properly?

If you’re using Odoo 18, efficient deferred revenue management tools and processes can solve these challenges.

But what exactly is deferred revenue? How do you manage deferred revenue in Odoo 18 accounting, and why is it crucial? How can you simplify the process of managing Odoo 18 accounting deferred revenue in a way that ensures accuracy, compliance, and smooth financial reporting? These are just some of the questions we’ll answer in this post.

Suppose you’ve been looking for a way to simplify Odoo 18 deferred income setup, better handle unearned revenue, or learn how to implement Odoo 18 revenue recognition. In that case, you’re in the right place.

Let’s dive into the steps and strategies to manage your deferred revenue in Odoo 18 accounting effectively.

What Is Deferred Revenue and Why Does It Matter in Odoo 18?

At its core, deferred revenue is money a corporation acquires or receives in advance for goods or services that will be supplied at a future date. It is an obligation until the service is rendered, and it appears as a liability on the balance sheet.

In Odoo 18 accounting module, deferred revenue refers to payments you’ve collected but haven’t yet earned according to accounting principles. As such, it must be tracked carefully to ensure accurate financial statements, especially for businesses involved in subscriptions, annual contracts, or prepayments.

Why is This Important?

Proper Odoo 18 deferred revenue management is essential for the following:

Accurate Financial Statements: Misreporting deferred revenue can lead to incorrect financial results. It may overstate or understate your actual earnings.

Cash Flow Tracking: Managing unearned income allows businesses to anticipate future revenue, ensuring healthy cash flow.

Revenue Recognition Compliance: Odoo 18 revenue recognition rules guarantee that your business complies with accounting standards, such as GAAP or IFRS, which require you to recognize revenue only when earned.

Without a solid strategy for Odoo 18 deferred income setup, businesses risk making mistakes in their financial management. Let’s explore how to maximize Odoo 18 unearned revenue handling.

How to Manage Deferred Revenue in Odoo 18 Accounting: Step-by-Step Guide

Managing deferred revenue in Odoo 18 accounting begins with proper setup. As discussed above, in Odoo 18, deferred revenue refers to the payment received from the customer for goods or services that have not yet been delivered or completed. This type of revenue is created or recorded as a liability on the company's balance sheet because it represents an obligation to provide the product or services in the future. As the company fulfills these obligations over time, the deferred revenue is gradually recognized as income on the profit and loss account. 

For example, suppose a company sells a one-year software license for $1200 and invoices the customer immediately. In that case, it can recognize the entire amount as revenue up-front since the service will be provided over the next 12 months. Instead, the company records $1200 as deferred revenue and recognizes $100 as revenue each month for the next 12 months. 

Let’s walk through the fundamental steps to ensure your system is ready for smooth deferred income handling. Let's move on to the accounting module to manage the deferred revenue.

Go to the Configuration > Chart of Accounts.

Type ‘‘revenue’’ in the search bar and enable ‘‘Allow Reconciliation’’ for the Deferred Revenue account.

Then direct to the Configuration > Settings.

Scroll down, and under the Default Accounts section, we can generate entries on bill validation or manually and grouped. So, let’s first select ‘‘On bill validation.’’ We can also choose deferred entries based on months, days, or full months, but for the time being, I'm choosing based on months. Then click on Save.

 After that go to the Customers > Products.

Then, Click on New.

Add the details such as product name, type, and price, and click on save.

Then, to create a new invoice, go to the Customers > Invoices.

Click on New.

Fill out the customer's details and invoice date, choose the product, add a start date and end date, then click Confirm.

The screenshot below shows that the deferred entries will be generated above. Click on the Deferred Entries button.

Under the deferred entries, you can find how the amount will be directed for each month. So, each month will take $100, and you can see how that will be calculated in the screenshot below.

Now, click on Reporting > Deferred Revenue.

The screenshot below shows that the total amount is $1200 for one year, and we will get a profit of $100 each month.

Likewise, we can also manage the deferred revenue with other options, such as manually and grouped. So, go to Configuration > Settings.

Then change the journal entries from ‘‘On bill validation’’ to ‘‘Manually & Grouped’’ and click Save.

Again, go to Customers > Invoices and create a new invoice. After adding all the details, click on Confirm.

You can see in the screenshot below the deferred entries have been generated.

Again, we must create another entry here, so let’s duplicate this. To do that, go to the Settings button and click on the Duplicate option.

Change the amount, choose the date, and select the start and end dates, then click on Confirm.

Now, go to the Reporting > Deferred Revenue.

The screenshot below shows that the total amount is set to be $1800 because we have provided the amount as $1200 in one invoice and $600 in the other invoice. So, it will be $1800, and we are getting a profit of $101.81 each month.

So, by changing the month by clicking on the above you can see the change in amount as well.

This is how we can easily manage deferred revenue in the Odoo 18 accounting module.

Managing Odoo 18 Accounting Deferred Revenue

With Odoo 18 deferred revenue management set up, you can leverage automation to ensure that the recognition process is smooth and timely. This reduces the chances of human error and helps you stay compliant with accounting standards.

1. Automate Journal Entries for Deferred Revenue

Odoo 18’s automation capabilities allow you to create journal entries when payments are received in advance. This ensures the deferred income is tracked accurately. The system will:

  • Move the payment from cash accounts to the deferred revenue account.
  • Split the payment according to your predefined revenue recognition rules.

Once revenue is earned, Odoo automatically transfers it to the revenue recognition account, providing real-time updates to your financial records.

2. Automate Billing Schedules

For businesses with recurring payments (like subscriptions), Odoo 18 accounting deferred revenue helps by creating automated billing schedules. For instance, if you’ve set a recurring billing cycle for a client, Odoo can automatically recognize deferred revenue monthly.

3. Track and Monitor Unearned Revenue

Regularly tracking your unearned revenue is crucial for understanding how much of your income is deferred. Odoo provides a detailed report showing the following:

  • Total deferred revenue.
  • The portion that will be recognized over time.
  • The timing for revenue recognition in future periods.

With this real-time data, you can forecast cash flows and adjust business strategies if necessary.

How to Use Odoo 18 Financial Reporting for Deferred Revenue

Once your Odoo 18 deferred revenue has been effectively set up and managed, it is time to view its effects through financial reporting.

1. Income Statement and Balance Sheet

Income Statement and Balance Sheet reports allow you to assess the recognized portion of deferred revenue, while unearned revenue appears as liabilities on these reports. They allow you to monitor the financial health of your business by showing whether the recognized revenue matches service delivery.

You can filter reports by consumer, product, and period to evaluate the effectiveness of deferred revenue management easily.

2. Deferred Revenue Report

In addition to the standard financial reports, Odoo offers a specialized Deferred Revenue Report. This report shows:

  • The remaining balance of deferred income hasn’t been recognized yet.
  • The revenue recognition schedule for each item helps you track when revenue will be recognized.

Having this report available at your fingertips helps you remain on top of your revenue recognition process, ensuring accuracy in your financial statements.

Odoo 18 Accounting Tutorial

Suppose you're new to Odoo or looking to understand how to better manage Odoo 18 accounting deferred revenue. In that case, several tutorials are available that walk through each step of accounting setup and provide insights into advanced features like customizing revenue recognition rules or creating personalized reports.

Whether you’re handling deferred income setup for a few products or need to scale it across your entire business, Odoo’s tutorials and community support can help you master the system.

Perfecting Your Odoo 18 Deferred Revenue Management

Odoo 18 accounting makes managing deferred revenue easy with the proper setup, automation, and reporting tools to help your business handle unearned revenue and revenue recognition accurately. From setting up deferred income accounts to using Odoo's advanced financial reporting features - this comprehensive guide equips you with everything needed for accurate, compliant accounting.

Odoo 18 deferred revenue management isn't just about tracking payments; it ensures your financial statements are accurate, revenue is recognized appropriately, and your business can confidently anticipate future earnings.

Stay tuned for helpful insight in our Odoo 18 accounting tutorials, and don't hesitate to ask any questions or share experiences with us at Netilligence.
